💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.
  • Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.
  • The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the manufacturer. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”.

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”.

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino notes that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an crucial part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”.

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”.

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”.

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the organization’s website.

#34032. Tech Report: How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

📅 19 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1571 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

📅 19 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.
  • But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects.
  • According to recent reports, the research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone challenges, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of latest ones.

According to recent reports, the research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone challenges, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

The lead study author said he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

According to recent reports, of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

In a recent development, first, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.).

Dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

Another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager says. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

Beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

According to recent reports, lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”.

Recent findings suggest that okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

Sources indicate that according to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager indicates.

Sources indicate that “When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall says. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”.

Sources indicate that over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager says. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

Industry observers note that in short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager claims. That stated, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

Resistance training is notable for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall indicates. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

Industry observers note that if you’re upcoming to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager notes. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

Recent findings suggest that protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health issues (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on notable components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

According to recent reports, rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

It has been revealed that bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager indicates. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

In a recent development, on that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager notes. In truth, though? “The medication side effects are quite manageable when prescribed by providers who are well-versed in current practice guidelines,” she says.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this concern with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

“The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” said Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”.

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”.

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

“Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” noted Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”.

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

According to recent reports, according to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-upcoming condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”.

To learn more, visit Framery’s website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s newly introduced function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS noted this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “notable conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

#34027. For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

📅 20 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1731 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

For Some Women, Weight Loss Drugs Are a Secret They Keep From Their Partners

📅 20 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends.
  • “I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF.
  • In a recent development, so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first time Caroline went on Wegovy, it wasn’t a secret: She told her boyfriend, mother, and close friends. Over the course of six months, they watched as she shed 30 pounds, going from 130 back to what she calls her “healthy original weight” of 100 pounds. Even still, her loved ones worried about the extent of her weight loss and didn’t want her to lose even more.

“I had tried every way under the sun to lose weight,” Caroline tells SELF. The 34-year-old, who lives in Montreal, asked to use only her first name to protect her privacy. “I was really tired of trying.” At five feet four inches, she wasn’t obese and didn’t think her primary doctor would approve a prescription.

In a recent development, so she went online and found a doctor who prescribed the medication over the phone, unaware of how much Caroline actually weighed. Immediately after starting Wegovy, she says, “the weight started coming off incredibly fast.” After six months she decided she wanted to stop. But as soon as she got off Wegovy, the weight came back: She gained 10 pounds in a month. “I realized, I can’t stop,” Caroline says.

So for the past six months, she has been taking Wegovy again, this time at a maintenance-level dosage. But there’s one big difference: This time, she’s keeping it a secret from her boyfriend and family. “Now that we’re talking about kids, he’s seen all the impacts [of the drug] and he’s done with it,” she says. Since she lives alone, hiding her medication from him is relatively easy—she stashes it in the back of the fridge, since it needs to be kept cold. But she’s still worried he’ll see it, and when they travel together, she has to hide the medication in the hotel room fridge—or, if they’re visiting his parents, in their refrigerator. “So imagine, I’m hiding stuff in my parents-in-laws’ fridge, hoping they won’t see them,” she says. “It’s super awkward.”.

Caroline isn’t the only woman going to great lengths to keep her GLP-1 use a secret. On a recent thread on the r/GLP1microdosing subreddit, women shared their tips and tricks for hiding medication from their partners. One stashes them in a tomato paste box. Another uses a play food container from a child’s pretend kitchen. Still others have turned to an opaque feta cheese container, butter stick box, anchovy paste box, empty bottles of women’s probiotics and Alani Nu supplements, a plastic to-go container, a metal water bottle, a box of wine, and a baking soda box in the back of the fridge—all to conceal the weight loss medication.

In a recent development, “It’s a real thing,” Kia Mitchell, MD, who specializes in family and obesity medicine, tells SELF. She has seen numerous women in her Jacksonville, Florida, practice go to similar efforts to hide their medication from their partners. The first time she heard about this pattern, it was from a patient who “just didn’t want to turn this into a debate at home,” she notes. “She just wanted to have the option” to take the medication. “A lot of my patients are similar,” Dr. Mitchell adds. “There’s this loss of control with the gaining of the weight, but being able to control the narrative around weight loss has been empowering and exciting” for her patients. “Because now they can reveal it on their own terms. That’s where the control comes back.”.

In a recent development, the reasons women want to reveal their weight loss medications on their own terms are palpable in that subreddit thread. “If my husband found out, it would just be a series of lectures,” wrote a user called Vivid-Act-6442. “Just don’t want to hear any negative or critical opinions,” wrote another user called [deleted]. “After 52 years of marriage, one knows one’s mate.” One woman chimed in to say she was hiding her meds from her teens—because she didn’t want them telling her ex-husband. “I just don’t feel like the questions,” she wrote.

Dr. Mitchell has mixed feelings about this type of secrecy. Anyone on a health journey benefits from having a “network that’s really cheering for you,” Dr. Mitchell claims. “Dealing with something like this, I want people to have community.” But, she continues, it’s “empowering and protective” for women to get to decide who knows about their weight loss drugs—even if, ideally, “you really want to be in a relationship with someone you trust completely.”.

From a medical standpoint, there are some potential pitfalls to hiding GLP-1s from a significant other. For one, it’s easier to get pregnant while taking them—Mitchell states she has “several GLP-1 babies” in her practice. There are also the drugs’ potential side effects, and hiding medication can make it more difficult for a patient to turn to her partner if she’s struggling. And more generally, secrecy can cause stress. “When someone is trying to lose weight, we want their stress hormones to be as low as possible,” Dr. Mitchell says. “If you’re trying to hide [medication], we’ll be fighting an uphill battle if you’re stressed about that.”.

According to recent reports, the bigger matter is hiding GLP-1 medications from your regular doctor, something that has become much easier thanks to the rise in telehealth companies like Hers and Ro. That’s a problem Caroline is having: She didn’t tell her doctor both times she went on Wegovy and still doesn’t want to, even though she’s concerned about how the drug may interact with the Accutane and Ritalin she takes. The idea of admitting her GLP-1 use to her doctor makes her anxious, since she doesn’t want to break their trust. But her annual physical is coming up, and her doctor will see that she’s lost a lot of weight.

“I use ChatGPT as my doctor at this point since I can’t be honest with my own doctor,” she claims. “I say, ‘Hey, this is my actual weight, what type of dosage is okay to take with other drugs?’” Admittedly, she adds, this is “probably not the best option.”.

Caroline got her Wegovy prescription through Hers. During the process she was only asked for basic bloodwork and received no counseling, just “documentation to read.”.

Craig Primack, MD, the head of weight loss at Hers, tells SELF that the company’s prescribing doctors “do ask [patients] to talk with their primary care doctor about the care they’re getting.” He acknowledges that the company doesn’t do much in the way of direct counseling but indicates that “we ask about mental health and anxiety and stresses.” The Hers app contains what Primack terms “psychologist-built information” about topics such as sleep management and eating personas.

In a recent development, dr. Primack is “absolutely” aware that some patients hide their medication from their partners. He says that some don’t want to say anything until they’ve proven they can lose weight; some don’t want to say anything because of the medication’s cost; some worry about how it could change the way they and their partner see each other. “Your weight and persona set up a dynamic in your couple,” Dr. Primack says. “When you start changing that, sometimes spouses get very jealous—‘Oh my god, you’re becoming potentially more attractive.’ Not that weight is directly linked to that, but that’s what I hear them say.”.

It has been revealed that and then, of course, there’s the more general stigma associated with weight and weight loss. “One benefit of telemedicine is it takes the bias and stigma away,” Dr. Primack says. “One reason we are here is because people are uncomfortable going to talk to their primary care doctor about it.”.

It has been revealed that whether or not Caroline decides to tell her doctor about her medication, she still will have to grapple with the larger issues that her Wegovy use, and her secrecy around it, have raised. “It’s very stressful,” she says. “The fact that not only can I not talk about it, but I’m also unable to get off of it. I don’t love the idea of taking medicine like that forever, but I’m kind of stuck with it.” She doesn’t want to gain weight, she explains. “But I wonder to which extent I’m too harsh with my criticism of my body. Maybe my goals are too intense.”.

In a recent development, given the incredible degree of vulnerability and sensitivity tied up with weight loss, the dilemma about whether to tell people about a GLP-1 medication is all too understandable. But how to tell people can make it easier, notes Rachel Goldman, PhD, a clinical assistant professor in the department of psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a clinical psychologist whose areas of expertise include weight management and disordered eating, tells SELF. “Framing it around their own experience and needs can make the conversation feel more manageable and less like something they have to defend,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that since deciding whether to have this conversation isn’t easy, Dr. Goldman would first encourage a patient to “think about their why,” she notes. “What led them to this decision? What does this treatment mean for their health and wellbeing?” Once someone feels more grounded and confident in their reasoning, “it becomes easier to communicate it with that confidence.”.

Dr. Goldman also suggests coming up with some sample scripts before having the conversation. “I would suggest that they lead with their own personal experience and not think about others and why/how others are using it,” she notes. “I would encourage them to use ‘I’ statements.”.

It’s also helpful to think ahead of time about a partner’s potential reaction and to have a blueprint in place for different scenarios. Thinking about what you want from a partner is likewise helpful—is it support, understanding, “or simply space to make their own health decisions without judgement?” Dr. Goldman asks. She adds that it’s important to remember that a partner’s initial reaction might not be their final reaction—it can take time for someone to process a conversation and to work through their own biases and misconceptions.

“Ultimately,” she says, “the goal isn’t to have a perfect conversation, but it’s to open the door to more honesty, connection, and support over time.”.

But if that fails, there’s always a box of anchovy paste.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio MASSIVE has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, MAJOR designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the fresh district.

It has been revealed that nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s latest Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,.

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a new development,” SUBSTANTIAL partner Sören Grünert stated.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”.

According to recent reports, the hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

Here, projecting bays and set-back terraces will help to create privacy for the residents, whose homes will overlook a shared courtyard.

MASSIVE used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

MASSIVE also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

#34022. Latest Update: It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

Latest Update: It’s Nia Long’s Moment—Again

📅 21 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day.
  • According to recent reports, I have just seen Michael (the new Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release.
  • On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a specific kind of vertigo that comes with leaving a movie theater in the middle of the day. The world is suddenly too bright, too loud, and slightly unreal. You have, after all, been inside someone else’s carefully constructed reality for two hours. And then you’re back outside, blinking into the afternoon light, not quite returned to yourself, the movie still clinging to you like perfume. It’s in this particular state that I meet Nia Long for an early lunch in a quiet corner at the Chateau Marmont.

According to recent reports, I have just seen Michael (the new Michael Jackson biopic) a month ahead of its April release. I’m still thinking about the film when Long, who plays Jackson family matriarch Katherine Jackson, arrives looking chic but low-key in an oversized blazer, wide-leg jeans, and a Miu Miu baseball cap pulled low. As we ease ourselves into the conversation, I’m struck by the strange doubling effect of the movie vertigo: the woman before me and the woman I have just watched, layered like two transparencies held up to the light.

On screen, Long plays Katherine Jackson with a studied stillness. The first time we see her, watching her boys rehearse, the frame holds on her loving face for just a few beats. She says almost nothing. She doesn’t have to. Juxtaposed to Colman Domingo’s blustering portrayal of Joe Jackson and Jaafar Jackson’s uncanny performance as his late uncle Michael, Long has found a way to make silence load-bearing. Restraint is the most visible thing in any scene she occupies.

In person she seems the opposite of restrained. She is blunt but also quite warm, with a dry sense of humor and a deep well of emotional intelligence. She is very much a Scorpio. She notices everything. And, in playing Mrs. Jackson (who is still with us at the age of 95), Long has tapped into the part of herself that knows how to let silence do the work. The word she reaches for when she talks about the experience of playing the matriarch—a word she will return to several times during our conversation—is grace.

In a recent development, “There have been moments in my life where I’ve been required to be more graceful than I’ve ever had to be in the past,” she notes. “And that requires a sense of really being able to dig deep into some sort of self-examination. Like, what do I stand for? What’s crucial to me, ultimately, regardless of Hollywood, the noise? And number one, for me personally, my children come before anything. And so I think when you look at Michael’s journey, and you look at Katherine’s journey, the only way you thrive and survive is through a tremendous amount of grace.” She pauses. “What I think I learned from her is that sometimes grace is really quiet.”.

Recent findings suggest that long occupies a place in our cultural memory that few actors do. She is, for a certain generation, the platonic ideal of ’90s Fine, a phrase that’s not only about beauty or aesthetic but also about a certain feeling. Watching her as Nina in Love Jones or Jordan in The Best Man or Lisa in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, you conjure up a place and time and attitude that feels synonymous with Long. Of course, there is the image, and then there is the human sitting across from me, eating her go-to order of salmon with a side of mustard. And as she does, I ask what she thinks about the iconography and the nostalgia that surrounds her.

Industry observers note that “My commitment to work is not for accolades or attention, or even to be famous, quite honestly,” she notes. “But I do think because of my commitment to truth and purpose, there is a thing, and I don’t know what that thing is, that people see in my work. And it makes them feel good. It makes them feel inspired. It makes them feel like they know me.”.

Industry observers note that in a fickle Hollywood landscape that’s even more fickle when it comes to Black actors, Long doesn’t take the longevity and love she’s cultivated for granted. “There's highs and lows,” Long admits. “I’m having a great year, but I don’t know what’s happening next year.”.

Recent findings suggest that long has starred in several iconic Black films, and she’s always been intentional about how she plays her characters. Much like with the Katherine Jackson role, she creates a version of the person that feels, to her, like something true.

Recent findings suggest that “The only strategy I have in this game is my bank account. Let’s strategize how we’re going to make money and create generational wealth. That is where I’m strategic.” She laughs, scratches her palm. “My hand just started itching the minute I remarked money. That’s a good thing. Maybe something’s happening. Something’s coming.”.

It has been revealed that once she’s in it, though, the work becomes something more personal. “I work hard to make sure that when I represent us, it’s not just someone putting their agenda on me. Whether it’s my hair, my makeup, my wardrobe, my lines.”.

Sources indicate that now that her eldest son is in his 20s and her youngest son, 14, is old enough to stay home by himself, the actor feels ready to expand in all directions. She wants to continue to produce more films, craft newly introduced stories both behind and in front of the camera. She tells me about a new film she’s just wrapped shooting in New York, Don’t Ever Wonder, a romantic dramedy (“If that even exists anymore”) three years in the making. It will feature her onscreen reunion with Love Jones leading man Larenz Tate. Directed by Eugene Ashe and featuring an ensemble that includes Blair Underwood, Susan Kelechi Watson, and Algee Smith, the film is all about second acts.

“This is not a continuation of Love Jones,” she emphasizes. “This is a continuation of love, and of what happens once you’ve had your kids, they’re off to college, and you’re empty nesters. And that’s kind of where the story begins. There’s a lot of funny and there’s a lot of heartbreak, and I think it’s a really honest story.”.

Industry observers note that in talking to Long, I get the sense that honesty and truth is what she values most in the stories she tells. It’s what she values in life as well. Perhaps that’s what compels me, somewhere in the middle of our lunch, to unmask. I mention that I am conducting the interview a little out of sorts, having just ended a 12-year relationship.

“Okay, but when was it really over?” she asks.

"You didn’t have to gag me like that!" I say.

Industry observers note that she laughs. I tell her that I am trying to imagine what life will look like—what I will look like—on the other side of this break-up. That’s when the idea of grace comes up again.

Industry observers note that in 2022, Long went through that peculiar part of fame where something private becomes public overnight: her partner’s cheating scandal that resulted in the end of their 13-year relationship. She doesn’t have to go too deep into it if she doesn’t want to, I assure her, but the actor doesn’t shy away. On the other side of the experience with her ex, with whom she now has a healthy coparenting relationship, she has an unflinching clarity about the whole ordeal.

Recent findings suggest that “The amount of pouring into myself that I’ve done is strong and mighty and intentional. I’ve now identified the things that I need to work on and the things that I need to heal. But I have also identified what is intolerable.”.

That clarity has been hard-won. When the cheating scandal happened, there was a groundswell of support from fans, a protectiveness over Long as a woman and as a cultural touchstone. But in the instances that she’s talked publicly about it, including in our conversation, I’m struck by how her gratitude for the support is always tempered with nuance.

Sources indicate that “I’m proud of myself for giving so much grace. For being able to say people make mistakes and things happen. It’s life. When the stakes are high, the news is big. I can’t do anything about that, but I don’t have to protect my ego in any of this.” She says all this very matter-of-factly, which is the only way she seems capable of saying things.

According to recent reports, in the same straightforward tone she suggests I write out everything I need to say to my ex without sending it, because ultimately “it’s not about another person’s behavior. It’s about your bottom line and the magnitude in which you’re committed to self-love,” she indicates. “I don’t think it's healthy to hold onto things because then you’re just walking around with this burdensome energy. It could be writing it down. It could be meditation. It could be prayer. There’s a lot of ways to manage the noise. But you don’t have to respond to the noise with the undercurrent of your own trauma.”.

I write down this last sentence because it is useful, but also because it is the key to something I’ve been watching Long do across the whole of our conversation: find the lesson in whatever she is given.

Long is working on her first memoir, a process she describes as one of the “biggest, bravest, challenging” things she’s ever done. It’s been a two-year process, a constant negotiation with her own relationship to letting go.

In a recent development, “I can read something I wrote two years ago and go: ‘Oh no, that’s not actually how I feel about that now.’” Long’s father, Doughtry Long Jr., a poet who died in 2020, told her the hardest thing about writing is knowing when to stop. “And I’m like: When is that going to happen? Because I haven’t gotten there yet.”.

According to recent reports, the memoir takes her back to Iowa City, where she spent six years of her childhood while her mother attended university. She was born in Brooklyn, in a Trinidadian household where everyone on the block was Black. Living in the Midwest during her formative years, she encountered few other Black girls, which disoriented her relationship to race.

In a recent development, “In writing this memoir, I realized the impact that experience had on my own view of beauty,” she notes. “And my own self-acceptance of being a pretty brown-skinned little girl growing up in Iowa. I thought I was beautiful because my mother remarked it and my family said it, but the world told me something different.” She lets that sit. “So to now be a face for Estée Lauder, it’s kind of ironic, because I didn’t feel beautiful until Black Hollywood said I was beautiful.”.

That an entire generation of Black women found a reflection of Black beauty in Nia Long while Long herself was still waiting to see it tells us something about how beauty standards work, and how much labor goes into transforming them. Nineties Fine, after all, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was a corrective, Black Hollywood’s answer to a century of the larger industry rendering Black women invisible or, worse, making us visible in ways that were wholly out of our control. Long’s most iconic characters—and indeed, Long herself—reflected a fresh idea of beauty, of the Black leading lady, expansive in some ways and still restrictive in others. Now, some 30 years on, Long embodies a new facet of being a Black woman in Hollywood.

“Black don’t crack” gets lobbed at Black women constantly, ostensibly as a compliment, but one that sometimes erases the very real pressure that comes with aging—especially aging on a public stage, especially when people have a particular image of you stored in amber.

Sources indicate that but Long is not interested in pretending that the body is not a thing that transforms. “I’m 55. I got hormonal stuff going. Your body shifts, changes. It’s a whole new body.” She is not wistful about this. She also ate the truffle parmesan fries and does not appear remotely conflicted about it. She mentions the coming press tour for Michael, how she wants to be in beautiful gowns but she also wants French fries.

“I don’t deprive myself of anything that I want,” she indicates. “I find the balance.”.

Beauty was never her primary currency, she states. It had to be something else, other inheritances: her father’s curiosity, her mother’s fierce self-possession. Tattooed and free-spirited, her mother wore leg warmers in the middle of summer because they matched her outfit, and she did not care for one second what anyone thought about that. Embarrassed, Long would beg her mother to take them off. She never did. As an adult, Long sees the power and freedom in that.

Our plates are carted away. Long has to leave soon for a pizza party at home with her youngest son and his friends. Before she goes, I ask her what freedom, at this point, is to her.

In a recent development, “Being able to do what you want to do when you want to do it, because it serves your spirit, not what everyone else thinks you need to be or should be,” she indicates. That type of freedom, Long adds, doesn’t require an audience.“You don’t have to have anyone else’s permission to do what you love. And it doesn’t have to be on the big stage. It could be in your kitchen. I know I have freedom right now to make a pizza. I’m going to do it.”.

#34019. How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1487 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

How to ‘Quiet Quit’ Your Mom

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting.
  • Sources indicate that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships.
  • Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you’re probably familiar with the term quiet quitting. For a while, that little phrase has been used to describe the experience of executing the bare minimum at work without actually leaving your job: You do just enough to get by but never rise above that benchmark to prove yourself or exceed expectations. It’s a strategy that can keep you employed while preserving your mental and emotional energy.

Sources indicate that the term has since been applied to other parts of life, like relationships. And, yes, it could also apply to the one you have with your mom. Though you’re probably not collecting paychecks here, maintaining a relationship with your mother may connect you to crucial resources you need to get by. Maybe your mom really does play a significant role in your finances, or she’s your source of health insurance. She could also be a connection to your culture or other family members that you don’t want to distance yourself from. Logistics aside, you might just want some distance from your mom without sacrificing your emotional connection. As I learned from reporting my book Motherf*cked: How to Keep Your Mother’s Toxic Drama From Ruining Your Life, those are all solid reasons to maintain a relationship that leaves you exhausted.

Going low-contact is pretty much what it sounds like: staying in touch with minimal contact. However, there’s no official definition, therapist Whitney Goodman, LMFT, told me in an interview for Motherf*cked. For some, it could look like avoiding one-on-one visits but checking in via text, email, quarterly phone calls, or greeting cards. Or you could catch up in person while avoiding the details of your life. The frequency of low-contact contact varies too. Some would say talking once a week is low-contact for them. Others might say once a year.

In a recent development, the reasons why people go low-contact differ as much as the ways it can look. Generally speaking, taking space can be useful anytime a relationship feels painful or draining. It gives you more time, energy, and emotional bandwidth to take care of yourself and tend to other important parts of your life.

It has been revealed that that can be especially helpful in our relationships with our moms, a dynamic that, for many reasons, is often packed with emotional triggers. If spending time with your mom feels exhausting, you’re sick of always stressing about this relationship, or you’ve tried and failed to set boundaries with her in the past, pulling back might be helpful here, Goodman indicates. If you can relate, here’s how to do that.

Ideally, this process is a series of experiments where you pull back from the relationship in different ways to see what feels good and what doesn’t, Goodman explains. You can then use that information to determine how much contact is too much—or not enough. Here’s how to get started.

Going low-contact is really just setting a boundary, or defining what behavior you will or won’t tolerate. You’re showing others how you want to be treated. Sometimes, people don’t like being restricted and get messy when limits are put on their relationships. Moms can be like that too.

If you’ve already tried to set boundaries with your mom by, say, not answering every one of her calls or telling her that you don’t want to talk about your dating life, now is a good time to reflect on how that went.

Sources indicate that moms who are receptive to those guardrails may be easygoing about any additional boundaries. That could mean you don’t need to cut as many points of contact to feel better about the relationship. On the other hand, if your mom has blown through your boundaries in the past, you might need stronger limitations to protect your peace today. Keep that in mind for the next step.

Industry observers note that again, there is no official criterion defining a low-contact relationship, so don’t get hung up on labels. First, think about how much contact you have now. How often do you spend time together? What does that time look like? What would you change to make this relationship less taxing?

Sources indicate that maybe you see your mom every Sunday, let her come over unannounced, and answer all of her texts—even the ones you’d rather not. Consider which of these interactions take the most out of you, and ask yourself, Would eliminating this point of contact make the relationship less exhausting overall?

Sources indicate that you could start small by taking a beat to check in with yourself before responding to your mom’s texts. If you don’t feel like dealing with her at that moment, don’t. If that’s not enough to preserve your energy, maybe you can limit the number of texts you’ll respond to each day or week. You can always change it up later by removing another point of contact, like those unannounced visits, if you need more space (see step five).

You don’t have to formally announce that you’re going low-contact, but giving your mom a heads-up might be useful.

It has been revealed that if you’re not worried about your safety and your quiet quitting tactics mean your mom has to change her behavior, then laying out your aims could make sense. Plus, explaining why you put them in place might help you resolve whatever is behind your decision to quiet quit this relationship.

That stated, if your version of low-contact doesn’t require anything from your mom, you don’t need to tell her it’s happening, says Goodman. For example, you can hold back information about your life or avoid certain events without discussing it first.

Sources indicate that feel weird about this? I get that, but here’s something to think about: You’ve probably told your mom about the ways she’s hurt you many, many times before, indicates Goodman. Even if you haven’t explicitly pointed to every single occasion she hurt your feelings, your body language and tone of voice likely have conveyed how her actions impacted you. You may be tired of retelling those painful events, which is why you’d like to avoid another confrontation with your mom. So consider this your permission not to.

Industry observers note that still, your mom might notice you pulling back and ask what’s going on. If she does, you can tell her why you’re not getting into your dating life or attending the family reunion. You don’t have to, though. You’re welcome to make excuses or just say, “Yep, you’re right, I’m not doing that anymore.” You don’t owe her an explanation.

In a recent development, goodman says the best way to tell how going low-contact is working for you is to check in with your emotions as much as possible. You can write them down in your journal, use a mood- or emotions-tracking app, or bring them up to your therapist.

Yes, the feelings you’re tracking can be related to your mom and quiet quitting her, but don’t forget about all the others, indicates Goodman. It might not be obvious which feelings are related to your maternal figure and which aren’t. After breaking patterns that existed for a long time, you might get a sense that something is off. Maybe you feel purposeless or lost. Maybe it’s like you forgot something on your way to the airport, but you don’t know what it is.

Industry observers note that all of that is normal, indicates Goodman. So is feeling like you really miss your mom, even if you know you did the right thing. Of course, everyone’s situation is different. Maybe you don’t truly miss her, but miss the idea of a person she’ll never be. When quiet quitting is working, those feelings should come up less frequently and/or become less intense. At the same time, you’ll likely feel some relief. You could notice more peace in your life and more space to focus on things other than your mom.

In a recent development, you can always tweak how much contact you have with your mom. Ideally, this involves a continuous assessment of what’s working and what’s not. If the low-contact plan you’ve established feels sustainable and makes you less obsessive or overwhelmed by the relationship—and your mom is able to abide by your rules—you might have found a solution. Success!

If this version of quiet quitting doesn’t keep your mom from violating your boundaries, emotionally manipulating you, or still leaves you drained, anxious, or depressed, you could level up, says Goodman. That means starting back at step one and quitting other parts of your relationship until you reach a point that feels sustainable.

According to recent reports, remember, the goal is for you to feel less stressed about your interactions with your mom. By finding a routine that works for you, you can protect the parts of your relationship that you love and lose the rest.

"All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
  • Recent findings suggest that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes.
  • Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the upcoming Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

Recent findings suggest that the beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the upcoming Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks.

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Industry observers note that sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

It has been revealed that that last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the massive deal.

In a recent development, A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

According to recent reports, that is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

Industry observers note that the architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Recent findings suggest that ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same complications that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

In a recent development, to be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many users, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers.

That leaves only a deeper issue, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

It has been revealed that inside, as Rem Koolhaas once noted, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

In a recent development, aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.
  • The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh says, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the problems that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

“I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Industry observers note that next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is at the moment weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she stated.

Sources indicate that the Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#34012. Surrogacy Nearly Destroyed Our Marriage. It Also Brought Us Back
