#33984. What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (975 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

What is the Ironman World Record? It’s Complicated

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Depending on who you ask, it's Magnus Ditlev and Anne Haug, who own the fastest iron-distance time.
  • After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.
  • That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Who holds the Ironman world record? Depending on who you ask, it's Magnus Ditlev and Anne Haug, who own the fastest iron-distance time. (Photo: Ironman (Donald Miralle), Challenge Family, FinisherPix).

After a dramatic DNF in the final miles of the run at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, Magnus Ditlev (DNK) raced at Ironman Florida just four weeks later to post the fastest Ironman finish time ever with a 7:19:17.

That time upended the previous best iron-distance set by Sam Laidlow just a few months prior at Challenge Roth, where the Frenchman finished in 7:21:04 on the course where the fastest women’s race ever is still held by Germany’s Anne Haug from 2024.

And yet, despite all these amazing feats, there are no world records in full-distance racing.

It has been revealed that confused? It’s understandable. Pour yourself a cup of coffee and get ready to learn why Ironman (and iron-distance) world records technically don’t exist.

In the world of running, 26.2-mile marathons must adhere to rigorous certification standards set by World Athletics that include restrictions on things like point-to-point courses, elevation drop, and (recent) International measurement, but triathlon operates without such official oversight. Course configurations are notoriously inconsistent, often shifting from one season to the next, and triathletes don’t even think twice about point-to-point courses or elevation drops between start and finish.

It has been revealed that certainly course distances are confirmed in high-level World Triathlon races like the Olympics, but there is no course certification for long-course or for regular age-group races. Often, you’ll hear athletes remark that their GPS watch clocked an Ironman course as short or long – rarely does a race hit exactly 2.4 miles of swimming, 112 miles of cycling, and 26.2 miles of running. Those are ballpark figures that races would love to hit if they can, but permitting challenges might mean the host city can only close 110 miles of roads for the bike course – this occurred at Ironman Texas in 2018, when “Ironman record times” were clocked by Melissa Hauschildt and Matt Hanson.

Beyond the logistics, an athlete’s clock is at the mercy of Mother Nature; factors like local climate, hilly terrain, or even a current-assisted swim can skew the data (as was the case in 2021, when Blummenfelt floated downcurrent to a 39:41 swim en route to a then “Ironman record” of 7:21:12 in Cozumel).

Because of that, Ironman confirmed in 2026 that they do not keep track of “official” world records for that reason, with a spokesperson telling Triathlete, “Due to variance of courses (even from year-to-year the same race could have course alterations), combined with the fact that unlike marathons, triathlon does not have official course certification for records, we use world best, course best, race best, swim/bike/run course best, etc.”.

The same holds true for Ironman 70.3 races and non-branded half-iron triathlons; no course certification, no “official” record.

Sources indicate that for what it’s worth, the Guinness World Records recognizes the “fastest time to complete an Ironman triathlon,” but not fastest iron-distance time (which we’ll explain in the next section). This may be more a function of marketing, as Ironman has established its own “partner” page on the Guinness Book of World Records website. Guinness does recognize some other triathlon records, including “fastest lumberjack triathlon,” which raises many other questions we’ll save for a different article.

Then there’s the branding gymnastics of Ironman™ versus an iron-distance race like Challenge Roth.

You see, even though Challenge Roth is a 140.6-mile triathlon, it’s not an Ironman. Ironman is a distinct brand of 140.6-mile races, though many use the name to designate the distance (similar to how most Americans say “pass me a Kleenex” for tissue, or “I need a Band-Aid,” instead of requesting an adhesive bandage).

And though Challenge Roth has been around for decades, the course and race have evolved. In 2010, the Challenge Roth run course was adjusted to be more spectator-friendly, and the bike course has been altered several times for safety, most recently in 2024. In 2026, Roth expanded the pro bike drafting zone from 12 to 20 meters, creating entirely different race dynamics altogether.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, establishing a definitive “record” is difficult even for a single event, given how much can change from one year to the next. And though iron-distance “records” are often broken at Challenge Roth, they’re technically not the site of “the fastest iron-distance times in history.”.

In 2022, Kristian Blummenfelt and Kat Matthews covered the 140.6-mile distance in what would have been record-setting times of 6:44:25 and 7:31:54 – except that they did it in a unique setup involving pacers, drafting, and extra equipment as part of the Sub7/Sub8 Project. The event allowed for advanced technological and athletic optimizations, featuring specialized gear like prototype bikes and pace teams on the swim and bike to provide slipstreams for Blummenfelt and Matthews to draft off of — all things you’d never be allowed to do in a legitimate race.

This format drew considerable criticism and debate on social media, with the community questioning whether the Sub7/Sub8 times should be viewed as legitimate records. Many referenced Jan Frodeno’s 7:27:53 time for a similar iron-distance experiment known as Tri Battle Royle, which was held on a highly modified course featuring special ramps and a perfectly mapped swim line to remove tricky turns.

Sources indicate that because these events were so heavily optimized, no one regards these times as actual world records — just like the much-hyped 2017 Breaking2 Nike marketing event for the marathon record. Instead, they’re chalked up to fascinating experiments for fans to geek out over. (And for that, we’re thankful.).

So now that we’ve determined there is no official world record for Ironman, iron-distance triathlon, or otherwise, we can establish there are fastest-known times, with all the caveats above.

One Bike for Everything? Our Editors Tested Hybrid Bikes for Daily Riding—These 10 Picks Are Best for Commuting, Fitness, and Light Trails

📅 23 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes.
  • It has been revealed that outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

It has been revealed that when I worked in bike shops, we sold tons of hybrid bikes. These bicycles are ideal for riders who say, “I need a bike that does a little of everything.” If you’re seeking versatility, a hybrid is often your best bike option. They’re a good choice for general fitness, commuting, running errands, and family rides.

It has been revealed that outside of cycling circles, the term “hybrid” often refers to vehicles that pair an electric motor with an internal combustion engine. However, in bike-speak, hybrids are a bicycle style that combines elements of road bikes and mountain bikes. Hybrids range from lightweight, sporty bikes designed for roads and bike paths to more rugged models suitable for light off-road use.

While they’re not ideal for die-hard mountain bikers or roadies seeking speed and the highest performance, hybrids work surprisingly well for many people on real-world rides. Typically, hybrids blend the lightweight frame, fast-rolling tires, and larger gears of road bikes with flat handlebars and the upright riding position of hardtail mountain bikes. Some hybrid models also feature suspension forks similar to those used on bikes designed for more aggressive, technical trails.

The Cannondale Quick 3 is our overall favorite hybrid for its fast feel and smooth ride, comfortable upright riding position, and reasonable price. These qualities make it great for latest riders who may be hesitant about incorporating regular bike riding into their routine.

Industry observers note that the Quick 3 features a comfortable Selle Royal saddle and Ergon grips. It also has mounts for adding a rear rack (the fork lacks rack mounts, however) and fenders to keep road spray out of your eyes and off your backside. While the pricier Quick 2 features a carbon fork and 1x9 Shimano drivetrain, the Quick 3 uses a steel fork and 1x8-speed Shimano system. These differences add a little weight, but the bike still has the gear range to tackle the hills on your commute or rides.

Cannondale also offers the Quick 3 with a step-through frame. It also sells the Quick CX 3 model with a suspension fork.

BUY QUICK 3 STEP-THROUGH - $749 BUY QUICK CX 3 - $849.

The CTY 1.1 (by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand) is a capable, affordable hybrid. The CTY is a great choice for a wide range of riders—especially for budget-minded beginners and commuters. The bike has an upright riding position (versus the sporty fit of fitness-focused hybrids). This geometry, along with a comfortable memory foam saddle and gel grips, makes the CTY 1.1 more comfortable than many competitors.

Sources indicate that commuters will appreciate the CTY’s flat-resistant, wire-bead 40mm tires with reflective sidewalls; they let you roll over potholes, dirt, gravel, random road debris, and even the occasional curb. For all-weather stopping power, REI equips the bike with Tektro mechanical disc brakes, and the Shimano 3x8-speed drivetrain gives you enough gear range to get you most anywhere you want to go.

BUY CTY 1.1 STEP-THROUGH - $649 $519.

Based in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint neighborhood, Brooklyn Bike Co. uses firsthand knowledge to design well-priced bikes that can withstand the rigors of NYC commutes—and the brand’s Roebling model is a great example. While the Roebling’s design is simple and understated, it’s entirely practical for commuting, fitness, and leisurely rides.

Industry observers note that brooklyn builds the Roebling around a double-butted cromoly frame. Although its skinny tubes look retro compared to the shaped, formed ones used on alloy-framed hybrids, the bike is lightweight (approximately 30 pounds), durable, and easy to ride. The Roebling features a 1x9-speed drivetrain with an 11-41-tooth cassette and 42T chainring. This gives you an easy gear for hills and a big enough gear for speed on flatter parts of your ride. Unlike many similarly priced hybrids, the Roebling uses V-style rim brakes. While not as flashy as disc brakes, V-brakes are lighterweight and easier to adjust.

According to recent reports, if you’re 5’6” or shorter, also check out the Lorimer. It’s essentially the same bike as the Roebling, but in smaller sizes (and in two color options).

In a recent development, want the easiest-to-maintain, rust-proof hybrid for commuting and riding around town? Then, Priority’s Eight hybrid is probably the best choice you can find. Weighing only 27 pounds, the Eight is lighter than many hybrids thanks to its aluminum frame and carbon fiber fork.

According to recent reports, priority originally introduced its iconic Eight commuter bike in 2016 but discontinued it after a few years. However, the Upcoming York City-based brand relaunched the model due to rider demand—and it’s a winner. The Eight features a Gates Carbon belt drive drivetrain instead of a standard chain; this system requires no lube or maintenance (other than an occasional wipe-down with a rag). For gearing to scale hills and overpasses, Priority equips the Eight with an eight-speed (hence its name) Shimano Alfine internally geared rear hub with a 307% gear range.

The Eight comes in traditional and step-through style frames. For all-weather commuters, Priority also offers the Continuum Onyx. It has fenders and dynamo lights that never need charging. Plus, it uses the Enviolo CVT (continuously variable transmission) rear hub. It has the same gear range as a traditional 21-speed drivetrain.

Test team member Tom Messina often rides the Cannondale Quick 2 for his daily commutes and on the local rail trail. He’s ridden it through snow squalls and on beautiful fall afternoons, and he’s impressed with the bike’s performance, versatility, and overall value.

Recent findings suggest that “At $949, you’ll be pressed to find many better options on a commuter or introduction bike than this one, especially from a brand I trust as much as Cannondale,” he stated. Messina particularly likes the bike’s low weight, wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. “It’s a top-tier bike for those getting back into riding after a long time off, or spinning the bike path on a sunny day.”.

Sources indicate that want a suspension fork? Cannondale also offers the Quick CX 2 for $1,099.

In a recent development, most hybrids use a road-style frame with a mix of mountain bike and pavement components. Scott takes a slightly different approach with its Scale Gravel series; the result is a blend of mountain bike and gravel tech ideal for adventure riding, backpacking, and commutes in foul weather or worn-out roads.

Intended “to go the distance over any and all types of terrain,” this adventure-ready variant of Scott’s Scale XC racing hardtail features an aluminum frame and carbon fork with multiple attachment points for carrying gear. The Gravel 20 has a SRAM Eagle 70 1x12 drivetrain that provides extremely low gearing, and Shimano hydraulic disc brakes ensure strong stopping power.

Sources indicate that while the Gravel 20 is probably way too much bike for most people’s rides, it’s a perfect option if your gravel roads and rides are more extreme than most. However, if you like the look of this bike and want a lighterweight option, Scott offers a range of Scale Gravel models—some with carbon frames and electronic shifting—from $1,700 to $5,500.

Recent findings suggest that this FX 2 earns high marks for its value. Its aluminum frame and fork have a look and feel of some of Trek’s more premium hybrids, without the added price. Internal cable routing keeps the frame looking clean, and like its electrified counterpart, it comes equipped with a Shimano Cues 1x9 drivetrain and Tektro hydraulic disc brakes. At just 26 pounds, it’s impressively light for a bike this capable. Keep the FX 2 as-is for a sleek, fast look, or use the rack and fender mounts for added utility.

If you want big tires for soaking up rough terrain, this isn’t the bike for you. The FX 2 rolls on 35mm tires with a max clearance of 40mm, making it better suited for smooth roads and cinder trails. But if you like a fast, efficient ride, this is a great bike at a great price.

According to recent reports, even though hybrids typically blend road and mountain bike technology and features, many hybrids are biased towards riding pavement and gravel roads rather than trails. However, Polygon’s Heist 2 leans more heavily on its mountain bike DNA.

Recent findings suggest that the Heist’s frame styling closely resembles hardtail mountain bikes, and its geometry isn’t too far from XC racing hardtails from only a decade ago. With a 63mm travel SR Suntour NEX fork and 1x8 Shimano Alivio/Essa drivetrain, you can take the Heist on light-duty singletrack. (Though you might want tires knobbier than the stock WTB Riddlers if you have anything but smooth trails.).

Specialized has sold its Sirrus platform for decades, and that experience shows in this bike’s details. This bike embodies the “I need it to do everything” ethos.

The Sirrus features sporty geometry for a fast ride feel and a rigid fork to save some weight. Specialized equips the Sirrus X 2.0 with a wide-range Shimano Cues 9-speed drivetrain, hydraulic disc brakes, and 40mm semi-slick tires for some off-pavement use. The Sirrus frame also has mounts for racks (for commuting or touring) and fenders.

BUY SIRRUS X 2.0 STEP-THROUGH - $850.

Many “women’s hybrids” use step-through frames, or are men’s bikes in a different color. As one of cycling’s only brands focused exclusively on women riders, Liv designs its frame geometries and touchpoints (such as saddles and grips) to better fit women’s bodies.

Alight is Liv’s hybrid platform; Alight models feature flat handlebars, rigid forks, 700x38c tires, and an upright riding position. This makes the Alight comfortable and stable without compromising too much speed. You can use the Alight for fitness rides and commutes since Liv equips the bike with mounts for a rack and fenders.

Sources indicate that the Alight Disc 2 features a 1x9 MicroShift drivetrain, with an 11-46 tooth cassette and 40T chainring. This gives the Alight a low gear for climbing hills; however, some riders may find the gearing isn’t hard enough for flat sections of road.

Sources indicate that most hybrid models are traditional human-powered bicycles. However, some brands offer hybrid-style electric bikes. These hybrids feature lightweight electric motors and rechargeable batteries to provide pedal assistance up to 20 or 28 mph, depending on local regulations.

Sources indicate that below are two electric-assist hybrid bikes we’ve tested and recommend. For more e-bike options, check out our in-depth Electric Bike Buyer’s Guide.

Sources indicate that this relatively affordable seven-speed model from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat—and now even more so with hydraulic disc brakes on this revamped version. Push the throttle, and the Soltera’s brushless hub motor kicks in, assisting you more gently as you begin pedaling.

Sources indicate that the Soltera features disc brakes, an integrated light, and turn signals. The battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (a surprising feature compared to the bolt-on vibe of many bikes in this price range), which helps the bike blend in with non-electric bikes. Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a 46-pound package.

Industry observers note that many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds, so a sub-40-pound e-bike is rather impressive. Unfortunately, e-bikes this light are usually rather expensive. However, Velotric’s Tempo only costs $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight. Velotric achieves this weight reduction and low cost by ditching the bulky suspension fork and using a smaller battery.

Recent findings suggest that like most hybrids, and unlike many e-bikes, the Tempo features 700c gravel tires. These tires roll quicker than 26- or 27.5-inch tires on pavement while giving the Tempo improved traction on dirt roads and gravel paths. Velotric offers the Tempo in a traditional double diamond frame and a mid-step design. Both frames are available in two colors and two sizes.

Since riders use hybrids in different ways, brands make various styles of these bikes to meet their needs and budgets. Some focus on lightweight and speed, while others are more rugged and can even tackle some easier mountain bike trails. There are also hybrids with features such as racks, fenders, and lights for commuting and touring, as well as some e-bike models.

In a recent development, when shopping for a hybrid, I recommend first thinking about where you will ride it most often. If you will mostly ride on paved roads and bike paths, consider a hybrid that focuses on low weight and has slick tires. If you’re commuting, look for bikes with mounts for racks or fenders, and have heavy-duty tires and wheels. For gravel paths or light-duty trail riding, consider hybrid models with suspension forks and knobbier tires.

According to recent reports, lastly, I always remind hybrid shoppers to consider a bike’s long-term use. Look for hybrids that use common, universal-sized components and avoid those with proprietary features or gimmicks. Riders often own their hybrids for several years, sometimes decades. You’ll want to be able to service and repair the bike down the line, especially if you use it for commuting.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#33981. The Best Gravel Riding Pockets in the U.S.—Including One Unexpected Sleeper Spot

📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1191 w)

The Best Gravel Riding Pockets in the U.S.—Including One Unexpected Sleeper Spot

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve been invited on gravel rides that range from a mix of road and well-maintained rail trail to rides where I wished I had a hardtail mountain bike.
  • It has been revealed that there are many people I talk to who say they have the best places to ride gravel.
  • Industry observers note that the definition of gravel typically exists between well-maintained packed gravel that feels like a road to singletrack that has some gravel between the more technical bits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been invited on gravel rides that range from a mix of road and well-maintained rail trail to rides where I wished I had a hardtail mountain bike. Admittedly, I’ve been the ringleader on more than one occasion for a solidly underbiked ride that was listed as a gravel ride.

It has been revealed that there are many people I talk to who say they have the best places to ride gravel. Some pride themselves on challenging and chunky gravel roads, while other places have gravel rides with a 10,000-foot view. And how each rider defines gravel will be different from person to person.

Industry observers note that the definition of gravel typically exists between well-maintained packed gravel that feels like a road to singletrack that has some gravel between the more technical bits. Many areas of the country may boast one great gravel quality, but this list compiles the places that check off more than a few boxes.

In a recent development, at this point, it’s clear gravel riding is here to stay, but the challenge lies in deciding where to ride first. Our list has the best gravel riding pockets in the country and can serve as your checklist for 2027. The last destination on the list is a sleeper you shouldn’t miss.

In a recent development, the New York Times featured a run-down of the best spots in the U.S. for gravel biking, so you know it’s now officially mainstream. Their list included Northwest Arkansas, namely Bentonville—in the heart of the Ozark Mountains—which has become known as a gravel (and all things biking) hub. That’s thanks in large part to the Walton family. The Waltons own Walmart and run the Walton Family Foundation, which has always prioritized bikes and outdoor recreation.

According to recent reports, if you’re in the area, there are endless ways to spend a day on a bike. According to the NYT, Chuck Campbell, an environmental manager for a wastewater recycling manufacturer, has designed several epic loops that together make up the 1,200-mile Arkansas High Country Route, a mix of paved and unpaved roads that launched in 2019.

Colorado might be home to the unique gravel races of any state, but if you’re looking for gravel events you can likely find one in just about any state these days. Steamboat Springs launched SBT GRVL in 2019. They’ve since grown to be one of the most inclusive events out there, with all kinds of training ride opportunities, and partnerships with inclusive cycling groups such as All Bodies on Bikes and Ride for Racial Justice.

If you’re looking for a quieter way to enjoy Colorado gravel, check out Nederland, a quaint mountain town 30 minutes outside of Boulder. There are probably more gravel roads in and around Nederland than paved, and almost all of them take you to excellent cafes and snack shops to recharge. Nederland to Gold Hill with a homemade slice of pie from the Gold Hill Store is tough to beat.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a way to escape the cold in the coming months, Arizona offers tons of gravel-friendly riding. Many of the multiuse trails around the Phoenix State Parks can be connected for some hearty loops. AZ Gravel Rides has compiled an excellent list of gravel adventures in all areas of the state.

Sources indicate that patagonia, Arizona, has become a not-so-secret winter escape for gravel lovers lately. Located in the Patagonia Mountains, it’s got a desert mountain feel, with plenty of climbing and lots of sandy roads with incredible views. The area is expansive, so you can ride all day without seeing anyone. According to the NYT, “a new edition in the expanding “Gravel Adventure Field Guide” series focuses on routes in Patagonia and surrounding Santa Cruz County.”.

Sources indicate that and on the East Coast, Vermont can’t be beat. Most people in Vermont will probably tell you that they prefer dirt roads to paved ones. There’s something nice about a slower pace. Seven Days VT claims that Vermont has 8,579 miles of unpaved roads, compared to 7,182 miles of paved roads.

It has been revealed that the VTXL is a 300-mile route that stretches from Canada to Massachusetts via 90 percent dirt and gravel roads. Former WorldTour rider turned adventure/gravel pro Ted King is currently bikepacking the route that he’s done before in a single push. This time he’s documenting the summer’s flooding that ravaged the state. “Heartbreaking but with short memories, we want to help bring attention to just how devastating it was and continues to be as Vermont rebuilds,” he posted to social media.

The gravel in Vermont is extensive, but make sure you tie in a climb up the road dubbed, “the steepest paved mile in the U.S..” Lincoln Gap may be known for having the steepest paved mile in the US, but the descent down from the climb is high quality gravel. Just a heads up—if you’re a fan of breweries, then strategy for more stops than you would normally expect.

When I think of a great area for riding gravel there are some factors that the location needs to have. Hard gravel climbs with ripping descents, some views while you catch your breath on top of the climbs, and something for everyone to ride—regardless of skill level, are a few things that top my list. Northern Pennsylvania may not be among the top areas for gravel riding for many people, but it should be.

Recent findings suggest that rail trails like the Pine Creek Rail Trail leave an option for anyone to get out on gravel in this area, but there are plenty of options for the seasoned cyclists as well. Events like Endless Mountains, Unpaved Pennsylvania, and Lu Lacka Wyco Hundo boast routes from 50 miles to 430 miles long. For context—the 115-mile route of Endless Mountains had over 12,000 feet of climbing. A large majority of the route was on gravel with very little stretches of paved country roads.

While the views from the top of the hills are beautiful its worth noting you don’t have the vistas of other locations like Colorado or Arizona. The area makes up for it’s lack of high alpine overlooks or desert landscapes with tough, punchy gravel climbs and positive vibes from the locals. Make sure this unexpected gravel honey hole ends up on your destination list for 2027. If you think I missed a spot (or have somewhere I should add for my 2027 ride list), then drop it in the comments below.

Micah Ling is a freelance writer who lives in the mountains of Colorado. She splits her free time between mountain biking and trail running.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#33980. 5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2453 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.
  • Recent findings suggest that A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants.
  • It has been revealed that this doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.

Recent findings suggest that A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants. Individuals in the first group were between 65 and 75 years old, and those in the second group were 85 years and older. Neither group had engaged in resistance training for at least six months. After following a 12-week strength-training program, both cohorts showed significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance.

It has been revealed that this doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell. Age-related sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and function, can begin in your 30s, says Robert Linkul, C.S.C.S., owner of Training The Older Adult. And it only ramps up with every passing decade. “There’s a constant battle against sarcopenia,” he tells Bicycling. “But if you resistance train your entire life, your body shouldn’t change drastically. Naturally, you’ll lose some muscle mass. There’s going to be some degeneration of performance and power output. But as long as you keep trying to maintain it, you’ll have it.”.

Julie Logue, M.P.H., senior program manager for Silver Sneakers, agrees that strength training is particularly worthwhile for seniors. “As muscular strength and endurance improves, you can perform activities of daily living with greater ease,” she states, noting that a regular resistance training program can also help older individuals maintain bone density, improve balance, reduce the risk of falling, and correct muscle imbalances. “Because cycling uses some parts of the body more than others, strength training is a necessary complement to promote muscle balance and reduce overuse injuries. Increasing strength can also benefit cyclists by increasing overall endurance and postural control,” she says.

Sources indicate that convinced but not sure where to start? With Linkul’s help, we put together five strength-training workouts you can do on cross-training days. Each one includes senior-appropriate exercises, some of which can be modified or progressed depending on your skill level and experience. For exercises that require added resistance, choose a load that’s heavy but doable; on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being your max effort, aim for between a 6 and 7.

Sources indicate that cyclists who are entirely latest to strength training want to go lighter at first. “Beginning with bodyweight movements can help build a foundation for using external resistance,” Logue claims. She also recommends consulting a primary care provider before starting any new exercise program.

Recent findings suggest that like most bodyweight workouts, you can do this full-body circuit anywhere, making it a convenient option for when you’re traveling, can’t get to the gym, or just don’t feel like dealing with a bunch of equipment. You’ll work every major muscle group, including your deep core, and train functional, everyday movement patterns, like standing from a sitting position, pushing up from the floor, and maintaining balance and control while stepping backward.

Industry observers note that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a chair, box, or bench.

Stand in front of a chair, box, or bench with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Tap the chair with glutes. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and body forming straight line from head to feet. Drive right foot to chest. Step back to plank. Repeat on left side. Continue alternating. Do 15 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward. Repeat, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start faceup with arms at sides, legs together, and feet on an elevated surface, like a small box, bench, or chair. Engage core and lift hips off ground so body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders. (Head and shoulders stay on ground, like a straight-leg glute bridge.) Allow arms to rest on ground or, for added difficulty, lift them off floor so elbows are straight and fingertips point up. Hold for 30-60 seconds.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

According to recent reports, start in plank position, shoulders over wrists and forming straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows, lowering body to floor while maintaining straight line. Press back up to plank. Repeat. Do 12 reps. Perform on knees or with hands against wall to make it easier.

In a recent development, this workout develops core strength through exercises that challenge your balance and train transferable skills, like carrying a heavy load, crawling in multiple directions, and shifting your body weight from a lying-down position. The single-leg glute bridge and superman variation fire up the posterior chain, which is critical for cyclists, and the three-way toe tap will help improve your overall balance and stability.

Industry observers note that perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a dumbbell or kettlebell.

According to recent reports, start on hands and knees, shoulders over wrists and knees under hips. Lift knees just about an inch off floor. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the right. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot backward. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the left. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot forward. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps.

Industry observers note that stand with feet together. Send hips back, back flat and core engage, to lower into a shallow hinge position. Keeping weight on left leg, tap right foot forward, then back to left foot. Tap right foot out to the side, then back to left foot. Tap right foot backward, then back to left foot. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Tap right hand to left shoulder. Then return to plank. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand, stand tall with shoulders back, chin parallel to the floor, and arms straight down at sides. Keep shoulders over hips (be careful not to lean away from weighted arm) and relax shoulders as you slowly walk forward for 30-60 seconds. Repeat, holding weight on opposite side.

Sources indicate that lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted, arms down by sides. Lift and straighten right leg, knees in line. Drive through left foot to lift hips up. Pause, then slowly lower back down. Lift with glutes and hamstrings, rather than low back. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

It has been revealed that A dedicated upper-body workout counteracts the time cyclists spend leaning forward in a rounded position and can help correct postural issues, alleviate back pain, and lead to better performance on the bike. This workout includes both pushing and pulling movement patterns and targets the muscles of the chest, back, shoulders, arms, and core.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, and a medicine ball.

Lie faceup on a bench or mat, knees bent and feet planted, holding a dumbbell in each hand, held above shoulders. Slowly lower weights toward chest, bending elbows, with elbows about 45 degrees from torso. Press weights back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg bent or straight (whatever is more comfortable). Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand, arm extended down in front of you. This is the starting position. Row weight to hip by pulling elbow back and keeping it close to side. Keep shoulders down and back, back flat, and core engaged. Extended arm back down slowly to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

According to recent reports, stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders with elbows bent and palms facing each other. Press weights overhead, extending arms. Slowly lower back down to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Recent findings suggest that start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg straight. Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand at hip with elbow bent. This is the starting position. Straighten right arm back behind you, extending elbow. Bend elbow to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

According to recent reports, stand with feet shoulder-width apart in front of a wall, a little farther than arm’s length away, slight bend in knees, holding a medicine ball at chest. Toss medicine ball toward wall. Catch. Repeat. Do 8 reps.

Sources indicate that strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, quads, and calves can help cyclists unlock (and maintain) the muscular power and endurance needed to tackle hills, power through speed intervals, and resist fatigue on long rides. It can also improve your movement quality off the bike. “A comprehensive lower-body strength and mobility routine can help ensure muscle balance through the low back, hip, and knee, all necessary for maintaining appropriate gait and postural control,” Logue states.

According to recent reports, perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, a box, and a hex bar.

Stand inside the hex bar, feet hip-width apart, toes forward. (Or hold a dumbbell in each hand down in front of you.) Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core engaged, shoulders down and back. Lower torso toward floor until parallel or you feel a pull in hamstrings. Maintain a slight bend in knees. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending hips. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Industry observers note that stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest with both hands. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Recent findings suggest that stand behind a step or box, holding a dumbbell in each hand, down by sides. Place right foot on top. Drive through right foot to stand up, extending knee and hips. Drive left knee up to hip height at top. Slowly lower back down. Step off box. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

It has been revealed that stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back, dumbbells framing foot. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted. Place one or two dumbbells on hips. Drive through feet to lift hips up, engaging glutes, hamstrings, and core. Avoid lifting with lower back. Slowly lower hips back down. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Industry observers note that if you want to capitalize on the benefits of strength training but only have time to train a couple of times a week, this full-body strength workout is the way to go. By incorporating compound movements, you’ll hit every major muscle group with just a handful of exercises.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps indicated, resting one minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and dumbbells.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Lift right heel and line right toes up with left heel. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, down in front of you. This is the starting position. Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core tight. Lower torso toward floor, slight bend in knees, until you feel a pull in hamstrings or torso is parallel to floor. Drive through left foot to stand up, extending hips and returning to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders, elbows bent and palms facing each other. Send hips down and back to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending arms overhead as you stand. Return weights to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

It has been revealed that start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and hands on dumbbells, forming a straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows to lower body to floor for a push-up, maintaining one straight line with body. Press back up. Row right weight to hip, keeping elbow close to side. Place back down. Repeat on left side. That’s 1 rep. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward, and at the top, curl weights to shoulders, bending elbows. Extend weights back down by sides. Repeat lunge, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating, with biceps curl at the top of each lunge. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent, feet planted on the floor. Hold a weight in each hand, then extend arms up, weights over shoulders. Drive through heels, engaging glutes to lift hips up toward the ceiling. Body should form a straight line from shoulders to knees. Pause for a few seconds. Then lower back down slowly, while keeping arms extended. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

#33979. Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

📅 20 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdfitness

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.
  • You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.
  • Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:.

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

Your body doesn’t have a cutoff age.

Recent findings suggest that people in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

Recent findings suggest that as a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

It has been revealed that that’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.).

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:.

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

But the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

In a recent development, you’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!).

Grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a newly introduced skill.

2) It takes way less than you think.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down.

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

Sources indicate that if you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:.

Industry observers note that I couldn’t have remarked it any better myself, Becky. 😊.

It has been revealed that no matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪.

Over a Tenth of Your Clients Are Dealing With IBS—And Here’s How to Help

📅 18 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1.
  • In other research, people with IBS noted they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.
  • In a recent development, some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1.

In other research, people with IBS noted they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.

In a recent development, some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth. These flare-ups can siphon concentration, interrupt sleep, and destroy work productivity.3.

As a result, many people with IBS plan their lives around the availability of private, clean bathrooms. Fear of a sudden flare-up leads some to avoid restaurants, get-togethers, even exercising in public.

This pervading worry has a name—gastrointestinal-specific anxiety—and it can affect everything from social relationships to overall well-being. It’s also the main reason people with IBS report worse quality of life than people with other chronic conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and end-stage kidney disease.4.

PN Super Coach Sarah Maughan, certified through Monash University—a global leader in understanding the link between food sensitivities and IBS—has witnessed how lifestyle changes can prevent flare-ups, calm GI anxiety, and allow people with IBS to live the lives they want.

“My hope is for everyone with IBS to know they have options, whether that’s turning to a physician for medication and/or a health coach to learn about lifestyle changes and how to put them into action,” indicates Maughan.

In this article, we’ll hear more from Maughan. You’ll also learn:.

Plus, if you’re a health coach, you’ll learn how to support clients with IBS while safely staying within your scope of practice.

Sometimes referred to as “spastic colon,” IBS is the most commonly diagnosed digestive disorder in the world, affecting about 14 percent percent of adults.5.

Unlike Crohn’s and other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), IBS doesn’t alter the architecture of the gut. When healthcare professionals use diagnostic imaging, they find no infections, inflammation, damage to the bowel wall, or other evidence of disease.

Years ago, this lack of visible disease led many healthcare professionals to assume that IBS was purely psychological. More recently, however, this thinking has shifted.

Experts now view IBS as a functional neuro-gastrointestinal disorder.

That means the nerves between the GI tract and the brain don’t function optimally, causing the brain to deliver unnecessary pain signals and interfere with typical bowel function.

IBS symptoms can come and go, with some people experiencing months or years of relief only to suffer a severe flare-up that can last hours to weeks.

In addition, not everyone with IBS experiences the same set of symptoms, which can make the condition challenging to diagnose.

The below illustration demonstrates the range of IBS symptoms.

It has been revealed that researchers are still trying to understand why the gut functions differently in people with IBS. However, they do have a few theories.

According to one hypothesis, the nerve endings in the GI tract may be overly sensitive in people with IBS. This can lead to two different sets of symptoms.

Industry observers note that ▶ Hypersensitive nerves communicate pain signals to the brain, causing people with IBS to notice digestive processes that other people wouldn’t feel. Tiny gas bubbles may be severely uncomfortable for someone with IBS, for example, but not bother someone without the disorder.

Recent findings suggest that ▶ Overreactive nerves can trigger GI muscles to contract with too much force, leading to gas, bloating, and diarrhea. If they underreact, the same muscles don’t contract forcefully enough, which slows the passage of food through the intestine and leads to constipation.

Another theory blames disturbances on the gut microbiome, which helps to explain why some people develop IBS symptoms after first having a severe GI illness like the Norovirus.

If you or your client suspect IBS, see a credentialed health professional.

Sources indicate that the symptoms of IBS overlap with several other gastrointestinal diseases and health conditions that can require medication, surgery, or medically-supervised lifestyle changes. These include infections, inflammatory bowel diseases, celiac disease, cancer, and food allergies, among others.

It’s especially notable to see a medical professional if you or your client notice any of the following:.

In addition to ruling out other GI conditions, a healthcare professional will also ask detailed questions about you or your client’s symptoms. This information allows them to pinpoint which IBS “type” you or your client might have:.

You or your client’s IBS type will inform what your healthcare professional recommends.

It has been revealed that A healthcare provider might suggest a short course of antibiotics and antidiarrheal medicine for IBS-D. On the other hand, for IBS-C, they might recommend a fiber supplement, non-habit-forming laxative, laxative-like medication, or other medicine that reduces the perception of pain and regulates bowel movements.

In order to get the most out of the visit, you can help your client (or yourself) prepare for a healthcare appointment.

A healthcare professional will likely ask the following questions, so consider the responses beforehand:.

Another way to prepare for your first appointment?

Well, you might not like it, but it’s a good idea to….

Consider keeping a poo diary for a couple of weeks before your appointment.

In the diary, track the frequency of bowel movements and other symptoms. Use the Bristol Stool Chart (below) to take note of the quality of your poo. This information can help your healthcare professional assess whether you have IBS and which type.

(To learn more about the clues your poos can hide, read: 6 reasons you should care about your poop health).

According to recent reports, in recent years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved several upcoming prescription medicines for IBS, along with a medical device that stimulates the cranial nerves behind the ear.

In addition, thousands of research papers have looked at the interaction between IBS and various lifestyle habits, with many promising findings.

Here are five evidence-based ways to reduce the symptoms of IBS (and bonus, many of them are great for enhancing overall health too).

People with IBS who exercise regularly tend to experience fewer symptoms and flare-ups than people who don’t exercise.

When researchers asked people with IBS to walk moderately for an hour three times a week, study participants experienced significant relief from bloating and abdominal pain within 12 weeks.6.

How exercise soothes IBS isn’t fully understood, though.

According to other research, exercise may reduce stress and improve mental health, which, in turn, may help improve communication between the gut and the brain.7 8.

Another theory argues that exercise helps encourage the growth of health-promoting gut bacteria, which may help to break down food more efficiently and decrease inflammation.9.

Anxiety, stress, and depression all activate stress hormones like norepinephrine (noradrenaline) and cortisol, which can:.

Of course, stress doesn’t come with an on/off switch.

Simply telling yourself, “Stop getting so stressed out!” won’t likely help—and may even paradoxically lead to more stress.

That’s why Precision Nutrition-certified coaches like Maughan help clients learn to focus on what’s within their control—such as practicing self-compassion, or experimenting with nervous system regulators like yoga, breathing exercises, and gentle walking.

As the image below illustrates, clients can control how they perceive, respond to, and anticipate stressors—but not always the stressors themselves.

Either way, when clients focus more on what they can control and less on what they can’t, they often feel calmer and more capable.

(If you want to help a client figure out just what’s within their control—and what’s not—try out our free worksheet: Sphere of Control Worksheet).

(Assess your current stress load by taking our free quiz: Do you have a Stress Bod?).

PN coaches have long appreciated and advocated slower, more relaxed eating.

Yes, slow eating helps people fill up on fewer calories—but it also tends to help clients reduce or even eliminate GI woes like acid reflux, bloating, and pain.

Recent findings suggest that for one, slower eating often translates to more chewing. In addition to mechanically mashing food into a pulp, increased chewing also allows the mouth’s digestive enzymes to pre-digest food. As a result, the stomach and intestines have to work less hard.

Plus, eating in a relaxed setting often lowers stress hormones like norepinephrine and cortisol, making it less likely that they will intensify GI pain signals.

According to Maughan, this can be especially crucial for young parents, as it’s not always easy to eat undistracted and peacefully when tending to little ones.

Sources indicate that (Sounds simple, but slow eating is more challenging than people think—and a lot more impactful. Learn more: Try the slow-eating 30-day challenge.).

According to research, people with IBS experience more shallow, less restorative, and more interrupted sleep.13.

Because of poor sleep quality, many people with IBS sleep more hours overall than people without IBS—yet feel less rested.

Fatigue can then set off a vicious cycle. When people don’t sleep restfully, stress hormone levels tend to be higher, which can exacerbate gut pain.14.

It has been revealed that unrested people also tend to feel hungrier during the day. Cravings for fats and sweets also intensify, driving people to reach for the very foods more likely to trigger IBS symptoms—and wolf them down too swiftly.

Stopping this cycle can be challenging.

As with stress, you can’t simply will yourself to sleep more restfully.

However, the first three strategies—exercise, stress management, and slower eating—can all help.

Some PN clients have found that consuming a smaller dinner earlier in the evening gives their bodies more time to digest before bed. Other clients tell us that a relaxing pre-bedtime routine—a few minutes of foam rolling, a guided meditation, a bath, or some journalling—tends to help.

(Find out the best practices for getting better sleep by checking out our infographic: The power of sleep).

While there’s no one-size-fits-all IBS diet, experts have identified several food categories that are more likely to be problematic for many people. These include:.

Industry observers note that ▶ Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols (FODMAPs), which are a family of carbohydrate-rich foods that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine. Even in people without IBS, these foods tend to slow digestion and attract water. When gut bacteria ferment them, they produce gas, which can stretch the intestinal wall. For most, this slowed digestion and gas isn’t especially noticeable; In people with IBS, it can lead to intense pain. High-FODMAP foods include wheat, rye, barley, onions, garlic, beans, dairy, honey, cashews, some processed meats, and many fruits and vegetables. (More about FODMAPs in the next section.).

▶ Caffeinated beverages and foods, especially coffee, which trigger the release of stress hormones, stimulate the production of stomach acid, increase muscle contractions in the colon, and irritate the lining of the intestine.15.

▶ Alcohol and spicy foods that irritate the gut.16 17.

▶ High fructose corn syrup and sugar alcohols such sorbitol and mannitol, which have been linked to gas, bloating, and diarrhea in susceptible people.18 19.

▶ Fatty, greasy foods, which can slow digestion and attract water, leading to loose stools, bloating, and gas.20 21.

If the idea of giving up all the foods and beverages on the above list has you in a cold sweat, know this….

Not everyone with IBS is sensitive to the same foods and beverages.

“Everyone can have different triggers,” indicates Maughan. “That’s why it’s so key to figure out what makes your body feel good and what doesn’t.”.

Sources indicate that some people struggle with apples but are okay with berries. Others can drink green tea but not black. One person might be able to consume five to eight ounces of beer but not 12. A gluten-free diet may work great for some but not others.

Similarly, many people find relief by avoiding certain high-FODMAP foods. However, you may only be sensitive to some FODMAPs and not others. If so, eliminating all FODMAPs would be unnecessarily restrictive and difficult to follow consistently.

For this reason, it can be helpful to try an elimination diet to see which foods and beverages are problematic—along with the quantities you can safely tolerate, notes Maughan. You’ll learn more about elimination diets in the next section.

(Want someone to walk you through exactly how to do an elimination diet? Read: How and why to do an elimination diet.).

In our online coaching communities, we often see people asking some version of the following question:.

“My client just told me that she has IBS. Am I allowed to continue to coach this person?”.

The answer: Yes, you certainly can.

In a recent development, as we mentioned, Maughan specializes in helping people with digestive problems. Coaching someone with IBS is no different than coaching a client with any other nutritional goal, she claims.

In a recent development, “Because IBS is often largely associated with what someone eats, it’s within a coach’s wheelhouse—with some caveats,” notes Maughan. “You can’t diagnose your client with the condition, and you should make it clear that you’re not prescribing a diet for them. In addition, you should encourage clients to seek care from a medical professional, especially if you suspect something other than IBS is going on.”.

To stay within your scope of practice, follow these do’s and don’ts.

Elimination diets do what the name suggests: They exclude certain foods for a short period—usually three weeks. Then, you slowly reintroduce specific foods and monitor your symptoms for possible reactions.

Elimination diets work a lot like a science experiment that helps you identify problematic foods.

The phrase “elimination diet” may sound scary and off-putting, as if you’ll be living for months on bland food you have to slurp through a straw.

However, there are many different types of elimination diets, with some much less restrictive than others.

This is an excellent option for people who suspect they already know which foods and beverages trigger symptoms.

According to recent reports, it goes like this: You eliminate up to four foods for several weeks. Then, slowly reintroduce them one at a time to see if your symptoms return.

Sources indicate that let’s say, for example, from experience, you know you feel bad whenever you eat dairy. On the lite elimination diet, you’d eliminate just dairy for three weeks. Then you’d reintroduce it to see how you feel.

If you’re unsure of how food interacts with your GI tract—but aren’t ready for a super restrictive eating strategy, our Precision Nutrition elimination diet is likely the way to go.

Created by PN and approved by several registered dietitians, the strategy removes many of the foods most likely to cause problems, while still including a variety of vegetables, fruits, starches, legumes, nuts, seeds, and meats, so you can continue to eat a well-balanced diet.

Industry observers note that to learn more, download our FREE Ultimate Guide to Elimination Diets. This ebook has everything you need to be successful, including an at-a-glance chart that helps you easily follow the diet, along with recipes, meal ideas, and tip sheets.

Over several years, researchers at Monash University in Australia have developed and extensively studied a low-FODMAP elimination diet for people with IBS.22.

According to recent reports, unlike other types of elimination diets, the FODMAP diet is a highly specialized form of medical nutrition therapy. The FODMAP diet’s list of problematic foods (shown below) is anything but intuitive, and the reintroduction phase is more complex than other elimination diets.

It has been revealed that as a result, if you’ve been diagnosed with IBS and suspect you have a FODMAP issue, seek the expertise of a FODMAP-certified practitioner. You can also download Monash University’s FODMAP Diet app, which will help you navigate low-FODMAP eating.

In isolation, more knowledge doesn’t always lead to more power.

For example, there’s a difference between knowing that dairy messes with your gut and doing something with that knowledge.

Similarly, you might know that you feel better when you eat a small dinner earlier in the evening, but you may struggle to plan your life so an early dinner happens regularly.

This is where a certified health coach can help.

“Many of my clients already have an idea of the foods that tend to cause them problems,” indicates Maughan, “But they’re nervous to know for sure because they fear that the knowledge will make eating more challenging.”.

That’s why Maughan assures clients….

Even if you do an elimination diet and you learn your favorite food is contributing to your IBS, you don’t have to do anything with that information.

You can choose to continue to eat your favourite foods if you want, AND you can choose to avoid them when it’s really vital for you not to experience IBS symptoms, she indicates.

“With knowledge, you have choices,” says Maughan.

Industry observers note that electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you quickly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

The Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

Sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. While only 33 grams and the size of an Allen key, Daysaver’s Essential8 has the same wrenches as your regular multitool. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

Recent findings suggest that what started as a homemade, low-sugar, all-natural sports drink is now a player in cycling nutrition. Skratch Labs offers a palatable solution that keeps you hydrated and energized without causing tummy aches. The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Recent findings suggest that want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. They also pack down to about half the size of traditional inner tubes, so they’re the perfect spare tube for your flat kit. They’re available in sizes that fit most road, gravel, and mountain bikes.

Sources indicate that we were skeptical that $40 shorts could be this good. However, the Black Bibs consistently outperform shorts that cost six times as much. They’re very simple—no fancy fabrics or creative cuts—and that’s why we love them. Made entirely of plain black Lycra with mesh straps and large leg grippers at the cuffs, they don’t look like anything special. However, even after logging over a year in the Black Bibs, one tester consistently reaches for them first.

Toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. Pearl Izumi’s Amfib model is a solid pick; plus, they are reflective for rides after dark. They provide enough stretch to fit over most road shoes (with cleats) and are easy to put on and take off.

Sources indicate that the small but mighty Mattone is a great choice for sleek, waterproof, and secure storage. Thanks to its elastic material, you can pack it to the gills or keep a minimal setup and cinch it tight with the Boa dial.

We look for two traits in a good seat bag: Carrying essentials securely without rattling, and mounting under the saddle without moving around. The Speedsleev Ranger 2.0 Small checks those boxes admirably. It has slots for repair items including CO2 and tire plugs, and a larger compartment for spare tubes and multitools. We’ve loaded it with two TPU tubes, a full-size multitool, CO2, and a plug kit, and still have room to spare.

According to recent reports, the Wolf Tooth 6-bit hex wrench multitool is a great gift for any maintenance-minded cyclist. With an optional key ring and a sleek profile, the tool is easy to carry on rides (or when asked to fix your nephew’s bike after holiday dinner). It has everything you need for most basic repairs. Plus, it’s made in America, with replacement parts available.

Dynaplug makes the best (and lightest) tubeless tire plugging tools on the market. The Carbon Racer comes pre-loaded with plugs and takes the guesswork out of fixing a tubeless puncture when sealant isn’t working. The Carbon Racer works like the brand's aluminum Racer Pro plug tool but uses lighter (and more cost-effective) nylon and glass-fiber construction.

Stan’s NoTubes is the original tubeless sealant brand and still one of our top overall picks. Most tubeless sealant was designed for mountain bike and gravel tires that run lower pressures. However, road tires typically need more air pressure, which makes punctures and cuts harder to seal. Stan’s latest introduction is optimized for road bikes with 50+ psi and claims to repair holes up to 7.8mm in size.

Sources indicate that A foam roller is a must-have accessory for recovery, preventing injury, and staying fresh. “I’ve been using this foam roller for years, and it's still going strong,” mentioned Senior Health & Fitness Editor Jason Griffin. You can use it to work out tension throughout your body, especially on the glutes, quads, and IT band. Griffin also describes a dual purpose for this foam roller: “I even use this as a balance-board base with an old skateboard deck for cross-training days.”.

Sources indicate that multitools are incredibly convenient, but can be hard to manipulate in tight spaces or when you need extra torque to loosen a stubborn fastener. This micro ratchet is a smart alternative that can speed up repairs and adjustments. It includes hex sizes: 2-, 2.5-, 3-, 4-, 5-, 6-, and 8mm, plus T10 and T25 Torx bits, a Phillips screwdriver, and two tire levers. Plus, it’s still small enough to stash in a hip pack or hydration pack.

According to recent reports, the machined aluminum Sport Mount is a great gift because it has everything we love about K-Edge’s products—it’s functional, looks great, and is priced right. The Sport Mount fits 31.8mm round bars and holds your head unit sleekly out front and aligned with the stem. Unlike cheap mounts, the Sport’s insert is replaceable if damaged.

Socks are always a go-to gift choice when you don’t know what to give someone. Luckily, almost every cyclist needs more riding socks—and Swiftwick makes some of our favorites. The Merino wool Pursuit crew socks keep your feet dry and warm in winter while providing cushioning and compression.

Industry observers note that if your giftee doesn’t already have a Buff in their closet to wear as a scarf, headband, or helmet liner, now is a great time to get one—it also works as a face covering when the temperature dips. The stretchy Merino wool fabric is easy to pull up over the mouth and nose as needed, and it wicks moisture to keep you dry.

Sources indicate that do you have a young reader in your life who likes bikes? “The Ragtag Best Friends Bicycle Club” by Marley Blonsky, a cycling advocate and co-founder of All Bodies on Bikes, tells children about Maisel, her sister Zoe, and new friends as she learns that riding her own way makes cycling great.

Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Fresh England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. How to Start a Workout When You Really Don’t Feel Like It (The Bridge Task Method)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself.
  • A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.
  • Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”.

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.

Recent findings suggest that A few weeks ago I was talking with Tabitha, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, about a challenge a lot of people face. ​ Some quick context: Tabitha is an executive function coach. She helps neurodivergent students and their families build the skills and systems that support their academic and personal goals. ​ And she noticed something: ​ The challenge of getting started on a workout is almost identical to the challenge her students face when trying to start homework. ​ This might sound familiar. You get home after a long day, mentally fried, and all you want to do is veg out on the couch. ​ In that state, getting up to cook a healthy dinner or go do a workout can feel really freaking hard.

Switching from a “YEAH!” task (chilling on the couch) to a “NAH!” task (workout/homework), is often harder than the task itself.

If we can make that gear shift less dramatic, it can make a significant difference!

That’s where bridge tasks come in.

Instead of going from YEAH! to NAH!, you insert at least one task that’s just…MEH.

I’ll let Tabitha walk you through it.

If you’re struggling to start your workout, don’t fight the gear change. Bridge it.

Add a little MEH to the mix and see what happens.

Tabitha put together a free worksheet that walks you through mapping your own task initiation sequence. Your personal YEAH -> MEH -> NAH.

Try it this week, and keep me posted on how it goes. ​ You got this. ​ -Matt.
