💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times.
  • According to recent reports, when shopping for latest road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a newly introduced helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

According to recent reports, when shopping for latest road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Sources indicate that helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

It has been revealed that so, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Right now, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

In a recent development, virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

Industry observers note that “The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” says Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

Virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a new helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

Industry observers note that all of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

The Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a newly introduced brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the company grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

The POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically big lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

Recent findings suggest that the Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

Recent findings suggest that in our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina said it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

According to recent reports, P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on remarked it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Industry observers note that unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

According to recent reports, ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

According to recent reports, of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Latest England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

12 Essential Things I Do In Every Yoga Class I Teach

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past challenges beginning in 1975.
  • I approached my earliest years of teaching with an enthusiasm that I hope helped make up for my lack of experience.
  • The following points express what I feel are imperatives for yoga teachers to remember while teaching.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past challenges beginning in 1975. This article about tips for teaching yoga first appeared in the July-August 1997 problem of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

I approached my earliest years of teaching with an enthusiasm that I hope helped make up for my lack of experience. As I look back now, in my 26th year of teaching, I realize that I have evolved a philosophy that shapes every class I offer. New teachers are usually so busy learning the craft of teaching that articulating a teaching philosophy remains a distant goal. Over time, though, we can evolve a style of teaching that expresses our values.

The following points express what I feel are imperatives for yoga teachers to remember while teaching.

As teachers, what we share with students can have effects that last far beyond the boundaries of class.

According to recent reports, the most crucial condition for a good yoga class is that it become a “sacred circle,” a term coined by author and Jungian psychologist Jean Shinoda Bolen. Each class must be a safe place for the personal exploration of body, emotions, and mind. A good teacher creates this sacred circle in which every student feels valued, respected, and completely safe.

The class must be free from verbal, emotional, physical, and sexual coercion or abuse. Without this intrinsic sense of safety, it is impossible for students to let go and allow the practice to unfold. In this context, safety means that the students retain the right to say no to working with a partner or to being adjusted or touched, and to say yes to moving at their own personal pace.

According to recent reports, look at each person individually and teach to that person in that moment. Each student is an individual to be guided, not a posture to be fixed. Often we focus too much on communicating about a pose instead of with a person. Your students might not remember the details of the asana (pose), but they will remember being seen, heard, and helped.

Sources indicate that humor teaches perspective and shows your own humanness to students who might otherwise tend to put you on a pedestal. It also enables you to reveal yourself, thus encouraging your students to reveal themselves as well. Laughter improves our breathing by loosening the diaphragm, and helps us to remember that while yoga practice is important, it does not always need to be serious.

I don’t like the word “correct” when applied to teaching an asana since it implies that there is something wrong with the students—that they are less worthy for not “getting it right.”.

In a recent development, “Correcting” and “fixing” a pose sends the unconscious and therefore very powerful message that “it is never enough.” Many of us are already slaves to this judgment. Our houses are never clean enough, our meals never organic enough, our teaching never sophisticated enough. By constantly correcting students, you tell them that, once again, they are not doing enough.

Use your words, images, and very light and occasional touch, if welcomed, to transmit positive information. We need to make sure that students don’t harm themselves, but we also need to communicate that while there is always room to grow, where we are right now has a wholeness and beauty to it.

Industry observers note that are we teaching students to become like piano tuners who never experience the joy of just playing the piano? Do they know volumes about the technique, but nothing about the joy of practicing it? Without proper technique, the benefits of the pose will be lessened and injury can occur. But if technique is all we teach, then there is no heart in our teaching.

Recent findings suggest that in the Yoga Sutras (11:1), Patanjali describes the dual concepts of abhyasa and vairagyam. Abhyasa, or “determined effort,” involves discipline, attention, and action, and it manifests as attention to the form of the posture. Vairagyam, on the other hand, is “supreme detachment.” Vairagyam is surrender, letting go, and allowing; it involves opening to the experience of the practice. When technique and form are balanced with heartfelt, free movement, then the asana is whole.

In a recent development, learn how to teach the same poses in latest ways. The basic poses, repeated in almost every class, form the bedrock of teaching. If you are bored with them, change your practice so you can find something new in each pose each time. Also, remember that while you might be bored, your students probably are not.

Recent findings suggest that we all need repetition; it is really the only way we learn anything. If you have taught for some time, no doubt you have had more than one student come to you in amazement to report a “great insight” about a pose he or she just learned from another teacher. You might have been teaching this concept for years, but suddenly the student was ready to hear it.

Sources indicate that even as you repeat familiar poses, include something newly introduced in each class. It need not be a difficult posture or technique. It can be as simple as a new way to practice Savasana, but it will nonetheless keep your classes fresh.

It has been revealed that “Listen” means observing with all your senses, as well as with your heart. Then teach from your heart what the students need right now. Do not be limited by what you think you “should” teach.

It has been revealed that no matter how much training you have or how many years you have been teaching, each class is a newly introduced experience. Trust your intuition about what is appropriate in this moment and teach that.

It has been revealed that for a couple of weeks after the San Francisco earthquake in 1989, my students found it almost impossible to practice standing poses. No one trusted the earth. Each time I would try to teach standing poses, students would have balance problems and become agitated. We all needed the reassurance of sitting down for a while. I responded to this obvious problem by focusing on seated poses, gradually reintroducing standing poses as it seemed appropriate.

Industry observers note that the body is programmed to move according to complex neurological and muscular patterns involving whole groups of muscles. We spend a great deal of teaching time trying to use words to isolate specific movements, when actually that is not how the body learns and remembers.

It has been revealed that when children learn a movement, they practice and experiment until they learn the muscle pattern which accomplishes that movement. Imagine trying to tell someone how to walk—explaining exactly which muscles to use as agonists, which as antagonists, and which as stabilizers. Walking is too complex an activity for someone to talk you through it.

In a recent development, nevertheless, teachers are stuck with using words until the student understands a movement from within. So choose your words carefully. “Invite,” “entice,” and “allow” have a very different feeling than “push,” “tighten,” “stamp,” “grind,” and “cut.” In a recent class I suggested that students “conjure” the pose out of their bodies. Images such as these help the student bypass the linear left brain and access the right brain, where whole movements are understood.

Try focusing on one thing in each asana rather than loading the student down with information. In the information age, we are overburdened with facts. We can know everything about the pose and still be unhappy in our lives. While knowledge about the pose can be useful and even necessary, it will not provide us with what we all crave: peace of mind, clarity, and compassion.

Allow the experience of the pose to be the true teacher—not your words.

Let the last part of the class be simpler and the sequence will be more satisfying. Sometimes it helps to have a theme—a part of the body, for example—to focus on in every pose. Whatever you choose, allow the instructions to become simpler as the students slow down and internalize their awareness.

Sleep-deprived Americans desperately need rest. Give your students the gift of learning how to relax at will by lying down on the floor in relaxation pose. I never cease to be amazed to hear from students that Savasana was skipped in another class and labeled unimportant. Nothing could be further from the truth.

In a recent development, studies document that relaxation lowers blood pressure and other physiological parameters associated with stress, including respiratory rate, galvanic skin response, and brain waves. Relaxation measurably improves the function of the immune system.

Recent findings suggest that savasana teaches much more than relaxation. It teaches clearly and concretely the importance of being, not just doing. Our culture is very much a “doing” culture; we value action and results over being and awareness. Savasana might be the only time during the week that the student is quiet and present—not acting, not achieving, not sleeping. This is the beginning of meditation and an extremely vital gift. Always allow 20 minutes for deep relaxation. [Editor’s Note: This article was written in 1997. We support a long Savasana! And it’s okay if you can’t allow 20 minutes for Savasana.].

According to recent reports, the integrity of a teacher’s practice expresses itself in several ways. First and foremost, it reflects how the teacher lives his or her life. Honesty in living makes possible honesty in teaching. A teacher’s formal yoga practice should be regular, not haphazard. But most vital, this practice should include love for yourself and your students, as well as love of yoga and life itself.

#33940. Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2526 w)

Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance.
  • How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.
  • Thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a newly introduced fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a newly introduced fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my big shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

Recent findings suggest that after finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

According to recent reports, “I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev noted, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

“Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he mentioned. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

Industry observers note that “There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the plans because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

It has been revealed that “That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that proposal. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

Recent findings suggest that sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

“It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

In a recent development, and for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Recent findings suggest that physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

Sources indicate that “To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

It has been revealed that “You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

Recent findings suggest that “I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before massive races.”.

Recent findings suggest that the day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

According to recent reports, “When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

In a recent development, “I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

Recent findings suggest that that feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

“It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

Industry observers note that thankfully for him, time went by promptly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

In a recent development, after that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

According to recent reports, recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

Starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a new world’s best time, the specter of the Big Island tempered his elation.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his fresh, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev quickly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a major difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of new cooling strategy.

It has been revealed that “It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

In a recent development, “So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

Sources indicate that when you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

Recent findings suggest that “We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

Industry observers note that A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he noted, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev swiftly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

“I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

“My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

According to recent reports, for now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev indicates he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

Industry observers note that “Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

In a recent development, “He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

#33939. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1311 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll promptly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • It has been revealed that if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll promptly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

It has been revealed that if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

Recent findings suggest that I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

It has been revealed that before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the problem in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

According to recent reports, A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the problem easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

Sources indicate that on a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

It has been revealed that I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar challenges early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the concern. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The tech giant has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

Recent findings suggest that if you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

According to recent reports, the significant problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

In a recent development, the easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Recent findings suggest that alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

In a recent development, and yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

It has been revealed that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Upcoming York City bike messenger but rapidly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

5 Yoga Poses That Help You Embody Gratitude

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the practice of gratitude can be a sticky subject.
  • Sources indicate that but at times, accessing that gratitude can be easier remarked than done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva).

Recent findings suggest that calin Van Paris is a YJ editor and certified yoga instructor. Here, she shares five yoga poses that can help you access gratitude throughout your body—just in case you’re having a tough time feeling it in your heart.

According to recent reports, the practice of gratitude can be a sticky subject. Certain events and times of year—season shifts, rites of passage, the holidays—prompt us to ponder the things in our lives that elicit gratitude. Life feels a little richer when experienced through the lens of gratitude.

Sources indicate that but at times, accessing that gratitude can be easier remarked than done. Global happenings and situations in our individual lives aren’t always sunny or sparkly, and we don’t always feel grateful. Sometimes we’re just mad, sad, frustrated, or over it—even in November and December.

According to recent reports, rather than convincing your head (or heart) to be thankful, try feeling it in your body first. The following yoga poses can help transform the sometimes elusive concept of gratitude into something more physical.

Spend a few minutes in one of these poses contemplating  gratitude. The rest of you might follow.

There’s something worshipful about bowing on your knees, which makes Child’s Pose (Balasana) an easy choice for this list. When you’re in a grateful state, thanking the Universe can become akin to a prayer or mantra, one worth saying over and over again. Spend some time here, with your forehead and palms pressed to the earth, and imagine roots sprouting from all points of contact.

In a recent development, another shape that finds you close to the earth, Squat (Malasana) is a pose of both humility and strength. Your feet planted on the ground offer stability, while the deep squat requires the cooperation of your entire lower body. Add the usual prayer hands, and Malasana becomes a demonstration of gratitude for your body, spirit, and anything else you choose to be grateful for.

Industry observers note that when you imagine a full-body expression of joy, chances are the pose in your mind looks a lot like Upward Salute (Urdhva Hastasana). The act of standing strong and lifting your arms in celebration mirrors the instinctive expression of wholehearted gratitude. When you’re in an authentically grateful place, expressing it doesn’t feel like a chore or an obligation—it feels like a party.

Opening your heart can also begin in your body. Bending back in Camel Pose requires a certain amount of trust in your body as well as in gravity. Once you’ve found stillness in the pose, your heart and throat face upward in a way that’s both vulnerable and liberating. Embracing this shape is a physical prompt for you to revel in—and perhaps exude gratitude for—the human experience.

According to recent reports, lying prone on your back is perhaps the ultimate shape of surrender. Savasana finds your front body fully exposed to the Universe and all it has to offer while your back body roots you to the earth. Stilling your mind and body here demands an acceptance of this present moment, just as it is. And if that isn’t an expression of gratitude, then perhaps nothing is.

A family of four (two adults, two kids) wants five nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, one of the flagship all-inclusive properties in Hyatt's portfolio. This is a beachfront resort with multiple restaurants, a waterpark-style pool complex, and dedicated kids' programming.

The Cash Price: During spring break, Hyatt Ziva Cancun's all-inclusive rate for a family room runs approximately $900–$1,200 per night for a standard room, all meals and drinks included. At $1,000/night average, five nights costs $5,000 cash. At $1,200/night, you're at $6,000. That's real money for a family.

The Points Cost: At 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night, five nights costs 125,000 points. You'll pay approximately $75–100 total in government taxes across the stay. That's it.

According to recent reports, the CPP Math: $5,000 value ÷ 125,000 points = 4 cents per point. At the higher cash rate of $6,000, you're at 4.8 cents per point. The World of Hyatt program's own editorial value benchmark is considered strong at 1.7 cents per point — you're earning nearly 3x that benchmark on this booking.

What Your Family Actually Gets: Every breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the resort's full-service restaurants. Unlimited alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from morning coffee to late-night cocktails. The resort's pool complex with water slides the kids will talk about for years. Non-motorized water sports. Evening entertainment. This isn't a stripped-down experience — Hyatt Ziva is an upper-upscale brand, and the quality of food and service reflects it.

It has been revealed that the Transfer: You move 125,000 Chase UR points to World of Hyatt at 1:1 — instantly — and book directly on hyatt.com. The entire booking process takes under 30 minutes once you have availability confirmed.

Book at the 395-Day Window for Peak Dates.

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance — that's about 13 months. For spring break, Christmas week, and Thanksgiving, set a calendar reminder and search the moment your target dates become available. Families who wait until 6 months out regularly find those prime weeks already gone on points. This is the single biggest mistake families make with this redemption.

Search Multiple Properties to Triangulate Availability.

In a recent development, don't anchor on one property. Run searches simultaneously at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, and Hyatt Ziva Rose Hall. Different properties have different award release patterns, and finding five consecutive nights at one property is easier than it sounds if you're flexible about which destination.

Use 5th Night Free to Stretch Your Points Further.

Industry observers note that world of Hyatt has a 5th night free on award stays benefit for World of Hyatt credit card holders. Book five nights and pay points for only four. On a 5-night Ziva trip, that saves 25,000 points — enough for one additional night. If you have or are considering the World of Hyatt Credit Card, this benefit alone justifies it for this specific redemption.

Earn Points Across the Chase Ecosystem.

Sources indicate that the fastest path to 125,000 points for a 5-night family trip is the Chase trifecta: Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (dining and travel), Ink Business Preferred (business spending at 3x), and Ink Business Unlimited or Cash (flat-rate earning). A family running normal spending through these cards can realistically accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually.

Don't Book Zilara When You Mean Ziva.

This sounds obvious, but adults-only Zilara properties appear in the same search results as family-friendly Ziva properties. Always confirm the property type before transferring points. Once points are transferred into Hyatt, they don't transfer back to Chase.

Points Expiration Is Activity-Based.

Sources indicate that world of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with a small earning or redemption every two years. A single qualifying activity — even earning 1 point through a partner — resets the clock.

Avoid Booking Refundable Rates on Points Speculatively.

According to recent reports, some members book award stays far out with the intent to cancel, just to "hold" dates. While Hyatt does allow cancellations, this practice can strain award availability for other members and creates unnecessary complexity. Book when you're confident.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption was designed — structurally, if not intentionally — for families pursuing financial independence. Here's why it fits the ChooseFI worldview so perfectly.

The ideal user is a family of three to six people who want a high-quality, genuinely relaxing vacation without the mental overhead of per-meal, per-drink, per-activity budgeting. The all-inclusive format eliminates the "should we splurge on dinner?" anxiety that can undercut vacation enjoyment. You've already "paid" with points. Just enjoy.

You need a minimum of 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For a realistic 5-night family trip, plan for 125,000 points — or 100,000 if you hold the World of Hyatt card and qualify for the 5th night free benefit. This is very achievable if you've been accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards through normal household spending on a Sapphire card.

This redemption is also excellent for couples celebrating anniversaries or honeymoons (use Zilara for the adults-only experience), parents of young children who want a vacation where the kids are engaged so the adults can actually relax, and travelers who want a warm-weather, beach vacation without the complexity of international award flight bookings.

This is NOT the right fit if you prefer boutique, off-the-beaten-path travel over resort-style vacations, you're a solo traveler (the per-person value scales poorly), or you're chasing ultra-premium redemptions like business class flights or city luxury hotels. The Hyatt portfolio has those too — but this specific sweet spot is about maximum family value, not maximum luxury status.

This redemption earns an **Easy** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. The ChooseFI community members who struggle with it usually hit one of two friction points, and both are easily solved. **The Earning Side: Very Easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers 1:1 to World of Hyatt instantly. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you already have access to the best transfer path. Earning 125,000 Chase UR points for a 5-night trip is a reasonable 12–18 month project for a household running normal expenses through rewards cards. **The Booking Side: Easy, With One Catch.** The Hyatt website is clean and the points booking process is straightforward. The one challenge is **peak date availability** — spring break and holiday weeks book up fast at the most popular Ziva properties. The fix is simple: use the 395-day booking window. Set a phone reminder 13 months before your target trip and search the day availability opens. **The Transfer Confidence Hurdle.** Some beginners are nervous about transferring points to Hyatt before they have a confirmed booking. The practical risk is real — if you transfer and then can't find availability, those points are stranded in Hyatt (though they're still useful for future bookings). The solution: always **confirm availability before transferring**. Hyatt lets you select dates and see the points cost before you're asked to pay. Get to that confirmation screen first, then transfer. If you can navigate a hotel booking website and move money between financial accounts, you can execute this redemption. Start with a low-stakes search on hyatt.com today — just to get comfortable with how award availability looks.

According to recent reports, check the same dates at the cash rate to calculate your cents per point value. If the cash rate is $600 per night and the award rate is 25,000 points, you are getting 2.4 cents per point. For all-inclusives, values above 2 cents per point are common and 3 or more cents per point is typical during peak season.

Industry observers note that transfer the required points from your Chase account to World of Hyatt. Transfers are instant. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, you can transfer directly. Freedom and Ink Cash points can be pooled to a Sapphire card first.

It has been revealed that complete the booking using your World of Hyatt points. Select the standard room type on points — all-inclusive benefits apply to all room categories. Add any special requests for your family (crib, connecting rooms, dietary needs) in the booking notes.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status (earned at 60 nights or through the Globalist challenge), you unlock suite upgrades (subject to availability), late checkout, and other premium benefits. Even without elite status, the all-inclusive base experience is exceptional — every meal, drink, and activity is covered.

Industry observers note that A 7-night stay at a Hyatt Ziva or Zilara typically costs 175,000 to 245,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 to 35,000 per night depending on the property and season). This covers the room, all meals, unlimited drinks, activities, and entertainment for the duration of your stay.

At Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) properties, children typically stay and eat free when sharing a room with parents. Policies vary by property and the child's age — generally children under 12 are included at no additional cost. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only (18+). Check the specific property's policy when booking.

You can, but you will get significantly less value. The Chase portal values points at 1.25 cents (CSP) or 1.5 cents (CSR) per point. Transferring to Hyatt for an all-inclusive typically delivers 2 to 4 cents per point — roughly double the portal value. For a $600-per-night all-inclusive, the portal would cost 40,000 to 48,000 Chase points per night, while a direct Hyatt transfer costs only 25,000 points.

It has been revealed that most Hyatt all-inclusive award stays include resort fees in the points rate, but you may owe taxes and some incidental charges. Expect to pay $30 to $80 per night in local taxes depending on the country. Some premium experiences (spa treatments, excursions, premium alcohol) may carry additional charges. Tips for staff are at your discretion and appreciated.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Industry observers note that hyatt all-inclusive resorts represent the single best hotel redemption for families in the travel rewards ecosystem. The combination of a premium resort experience, all meals and drinks included, and 2 to 4 cents per point value makes this a sweet spot that is hard to beat. A family of four can enjoy a week-long beach vacation at a Hyatt Ziva for 175,000 transferable Chase points — a stay that would cost $4,000 to $7,000 in cash. For the ChooseFI community, this is the redemption that makes points tangible: your kids are splashing in the pool, you are enjoying a beachfront dinner, and the entire experience was covered by your Chase credit card rewards. Transfer to Hyatt, book early for peak dates, and give your family the vacation you have been optimizing for.

Breaking: The 9 Best Fresh Balance Running Shoes of 2026, for Training, Racing, and More

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, editor’s Note, November 13, 2026: Our Best Overall Latest Balance trainer, the Fresh Foam X 880v15, is 23% off. There are also early Black Friday sales on Amazon, where you can get older models, like the 1080v14, for as high as 45% off.

Sources indicate that you might know New Balance as the preeminent source of dad shoes—those chunky, overlay-clad sneakers ubiquitous among lawn-mowing, beer-drinking guys of a certain age. Yes, New Balance still makes these kicks (and they’re actually back in style), but that’s just a small sliver of this company’s story.

Fresh Balance is a highly respected brand with a long history: The company was founded in 1906 in Boston and originally sold arch supports. Among runners, New Balance has a reputation for creating reliable training shoes with a strong emphasis on comfort. The Ellipse, which earned a 2026 Shoe Award, is a great example: It’s a cushioned, stable, bouncy trainer that works well for a wide swath of runners.

Sources indicate that in recent years, the brand has broadened its lineup beyond trusty workhorse shoes with models like the SuperComp Elite, a carbon-plated speed shoe designed for racing. Today, Upcoming Balance is on the cutting edge—no lawn mower required.

This guide highlights the top pairs in the New Balance stable. The brand makes something for everyone, and there are well-regarded models here to suit all kinds of runners, including supportive trainers, max-cushion sneakers, racing shoes, and even trail shoes. Read on to learn more about the key tech NB uses in its shoes and dive into our favorite pairs below.

Shopping for a neutral trainer → Upcoming Balance Fresh Foam X 880v15 (Men’s/Women’s)On a budget → New Balance Fresh Foam 680v9 (Men’s/Women’s)Looking for a bargain → New Balance Ellipse (Men’s/Women’s)Hooked on carbon → New Balance SuperComp Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)In need of a plush ride → New Balance Fresh Foam X 1080v15 (Men’s/Women’s)Sticking to the trails → New Balance Fresh Foam X Hierro v9 (Men’s/Women’s)Running intervals and fartleks → New Balance FuelCell Rebel v5 (Men’s/Women’s)Racing → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)Rolling your foot inward (overpronating) → New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v15 (Men’s/Women’s).

In a recent development, to write this guide, I talked with a New Balance brand rep and reviewed the firm’s lineup to learn more about its latest models and shoe tech. I also combed through Runner’s World reviews of New Balance shoes and consulted with RW Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer, who provided testing data on New Balance models included in the Runner’s World wear-test program.

I chose the shoes you see below, making sure to include models that showcase the best New Balance tech and design approaches as well as shoes for different running disciplines.

The 880 is one of Upcoming Balance’s core training shoes, and the v15 is a real standout: RW testers called it “one shoe that can do it all,” and it earned a 2025 Shoe Award thanks to its versatility and stable ride.

The 880 is a neutral trainer that features an EVA-based Fresh Foam X midsole. Newly introduced Balance bumped the stack height to more than 40 mm for v15, giving this shoe even more cushioning (at the cost of increased weight). But as Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate notes in his review, the shoe doesn’t feel pillowy soft. Instead, it’s surprisingly stable: The thick midsole takes the sting out of impacts and feels planted underfoot, and combined with the 880’s snug upper, the shoe serves up a comfortable, predictable ride that’s great for everyday training.

It has been revealed that the 880 is classic New Balance: a trusty workhorse that’ll keep your feet happy through neighborhood jogs and long runs alike (one tester even liked it for speed workouts). If reliability and comfort are your top priorities for running shoes, you can’t go wrong with this model.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

It has been revealed that this below-$100 shoe doesn’t skimp on comfort despite the low price tag. The Fresh Foam 680v9 has soft, supportive cushioning that’s great for everyday training. It’s surprisingly durable for accruing miles, and you won’t feel like you’re slogging because it’s anything but beefy.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe has an accommodating fit in the midfoot area, though some commented the toebox feels slightly narrow. You can go up a size—or up a width. The 680v9 comes in wide (men’s, women’s) and extra wide (men’s).

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance Fresh Foam 680v9 Review.

In a recent development, the Ellipse, included in our 2026 Shoe Awards, is the shoe version of a run friend. Meant to encapsulate the feeling of going on a group run, Upcoming Balance’s newest shoe has plush, supportive foam that makes your runs feel easier and bouncier.

Sources indicate that the midsole, Fresh Foam X, gets tweaked with new geometry (look ma, no more hexagons!). The foam compresses and promptly springs back upon impact, making the ride feel trampoline-like. But the Ellipse isn’t for speedwork. Testers commented how it’s quite bulky to run in. However, they enjoyed how the shoe put pep in their step during easy runs and recovery runs.

In a recent development, “The shoe is SO springy,” stated tester Laura Parks. “It’s like running with a strong wind at your back except the extra momentum is coming from the ground.”.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

We get it—you want to run in your carbon-plated, super foam shoes every day. Thing is, with the exception of a few test runs, you should save your super shoes for race day so they stay fresh. Here’s where the SC Rebel comes in. New Balance created a carbon-plated shoe specifically for training. It’s intended to make your runs feel easier as you reap the propulsion from the carbon plate and TPEE-based Infinion foam.

Recent findings suggest that furrer took the SC Rebel out on a long run over road and trail, and found the shoe’s traction reliable on both surfaces. “The shoe has a wider platform that helps with stability; it has more support than your standard super shoe,” she remarked. “I was impressed with the snap and slightly spongy but not aggressive rebound. I trusted the shoe over loose dirt and pavement pocked with potholes.”.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance SuperComp Rebel Preview.

In a recent development, the plush 1080, which we also included in our 2026 Shoe Awards, gets a major update in its latest iteration. The team swapped the EVA-based Fresh Foam midsole for Infinion. Composed of supercritical TPEE and TPU-based, Infinion is more durable and delivers a bouncier ride. This change gives the 1080v15 a sportier edge. Testers who initially mentioned it was too bulky eventually deemed the shoe as their upcoming daily trainer.

According to recent reports, “The Infinion Foam tends to hit that balance I look for in a daily trainer—it has some pop in the cushioning without being too soft,” said tester and Director of Content Operations Brian Dalek. “And it lasts a long time. I could easily go for easy weekly long runs in them, but also turn up my speed a little bit with them without feeling like I had too much of a shoe on.”.

Tester Nina Rems, who averages 25 miles a week at 7:45 pace, also commented on the responsive ride and how the 1080v15 doubles as an everyday running shoe and designated long-run trainer.

“I found these sneakers to be like ‘running on air.’ The springiness of the Infinion foam gave me a bouncy rebound each step,” she said. “I felt energized! I found these to be fantastic daily trainers, a sneaker I will continue to reach for on my long runs. From out of the box, these sneakers felt great, no hot spots to work through, just continued comfort in a not-so-bulky feeling.”.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

A popular and award-winning trail shoe, the Hierro continues with the formula that has won it such a loyal following: a soft Fresh Foam X midsole paired with a rugged and grippy Vibram outsole, now upgraded for v9 with deeper lugs for better grip on challenging terrain. Although it lacks a rock plate, the plush midsole does a good job of soaking up shocks and bumps on the trail.

Industry observers note that the Hierro v9 features a dual-density Fresh Foam X midsole: a soft top layer cushions impacts and creates a plush underfoot feel, and a firmer lower layer stabilizes the shoe and keeps sharp debris from poking up into your feet. The mesh upper is designed to breathe well, and overlays keep your feet protected from scrapes against rocks and brush. On the bottom, the Vibram outsole now features enlarged 4.5mm lugs for plenty of bite in the dirt.

RW testers gave the Hierro high marks overall, and they especially loved its cushy Fresh Foam X midsole: “For comfort over distance, it’s one of the best I’ve tried,” one tester mentioned.

Sources indicate that but a few testers did note a sloppy fit that caused their feet to slide around in the shoe on technical terrain and downhills. That means the Hierro isn’t the best choice for super gnarly trails, but for everyday trail running on light to moderate terrain, its cushioned ride is top-notch.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance has been steadily tweaking the Rebel over the past couple iterations, and the latest edition offers significantly increased cushioning while still maintaining a feathery weight. This is a great shoe for speed training, although it serves up a comfy overall feel that works well at slower speeds, too.

In a recent development, like the v4, the Rebel v5 features a blend of PEBA and EVA foams in its FuelCell midsole. The main difference? There’s more of it: The shoe’s stack height grew from 30mm in the v4 up to 35mm in the v5. The sole has a pronounced rocker shape, and despite the relatively tall wedge of cushioning, our testers said the shoe felt firm—but comfy.

It has been revealed that “[The Rebel v5] is just a little firmer than other New Balance shoes I’ve run in, but it gets the job done,” said tester Sean O’Connor, who previously tested the cushier FuelCell SuperComp Trainer. Despite the shoe’s firmer platform, O’Connor described the ride as “super comfortable the entire run.”.

In a recent development, the Rebel lacks the carbon-fiber plate found in its race-oriented sibling, the SuperComp Elite, so it can’t quite achieve super shoe levels of bounciness from its midsole. Even so, runners say it feels peppy, and its more streamlined sole design makes it very comfortable at a wide range of paces.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Sources indicate that latest Balance seems to revamp its super shoes every year, with no two models looking—or riding—alike. And we’re here for that ride. In lieu of FuelCell, the brand switched in a lighter and bouncier version of Infinion, the new foam introduced in the max-cushioned 1080v15. It’s a move we’re seeing lots of brands participate in, such as Saucony and Asics, swapping PEBA for A-TPU, or in this case, TPEE.

According to recent reports, this makes the SuperComp Elite v6 even lighter than its predecessor (although, all things considered, the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 was a chonk). To shave off even more weight, the upper is replaced with translucent mesh, which gives the shoe a track flat vibe.

Industry observers note that the shoe isn’t as aggressive as some of its competitors, and a couple testers found the cushioning firm. But the accommodating fit in the midfoot area provided comfort over long miles when testers’ feet began to swell. The plush cushioning in the heel was also a favorite feature, especially for heel strikers.

“Very comfy for long miles,” remarked shoe tester Josh Davis. “You can definitely wear these in a marathon and count on the comfort to last.”.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Fresh Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

Sources indicate that now on its 15th iteration, the 860 is a trusted workhorse trainer that offers a supportive feel and good cushioning for routine training miles. The latest version has the 14’s fresh last and rocker shape for smooth strides; it also includes the previous iteration’s Stability Plane, a thin, stiff EVA-based midsole plate that supports the foot.

It has been revealed that the 860 is built with a relatively wide full-contact sole, which gives it some inherent stability. The midsole features two flavors of Fresh Foam X plus the embedded Stability Plane. There’s a denser, harder layer of foam at the bottom, and it works in concert with the rigid Stability Plane to resist overpronation and support the foot. The top layer of the midsole is a softer version of Fresh Foam X that absorbs impact forces for a plush feel.

With its somewhat heavy build and comfort-oriented midsole design, the 860 isn’t the smartest choice for tempo runs, but testers loved it for general training, and it’s a great pick for those who need some extra support under their feet.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Midsole foams are the main technology that differentiates Upcoming Balance shoes. Like other shoe brands, New Balance has entered the foam wars by engineering its own proprietary cushioning foams. There are two key ones to know: Fresh Foam and FuelCell.

The latest version of Fresh Foam is Fresh Foam X, and it’s used in the brand’s workhorse training shoes, including stalwart models like the 880, 1080, and 860. This is an EVA-based foam that’s formulated for softness, and it gives these shoes a well-padded feel underfoot. Fresh Foam X serves up a comfortable ride that’s ideal for casual running and day-to-day training.

FuelCell is used in Upcoming Balance’s speed-oriented models, like the Rebel and SuperComp Elite, and it’s optimized for energy return and responsiveness. New Balance tweaks the exact formula of this foam depending on the shoe and its intended use.

Sources indicate that the training-oriented Rebel has a FuelCell midsole made from a blend of EVA and polyether block amide (PEBA)—a lightweight, soft, and very springy material that’s used in many brands’ speed shoes. This blend gives the Rebel a good balance of shock absorption and bounce.

The race-focused SuperComp Elite, however, has a FuelCell midsole made entirely from PEBA, which saves weight while still allowing for a very thick layer of cushioning. It’s paired with a carbon-fiber plate that stabilizes your foot as you run and helps you get maximum squish—and propulsive energy return—from the hefty slice of foam. The result is a bouncy, propulsive ride that helps you push the pace, and it’s a great choice for race day.

In a recent development, introduced with the 1080v15, Infinion foam is lighter and bouncier than the brand’s Fresh Foam X. New Balance has also tweaked Infinion for its racing collection of shoes. The TPEE-based foam in the SuperComp Elite v6 and SC Rebel delivers higher rebound, working with the rocker profile to encourage fast turnover, and the Energy Arc carbon plate, which helps stabilize the foam and provides propulsion.

Sources indicate that for decades, Latest Balance has used a number system to name its shoes—you’re probably familiar with classic models like the 990. The number system encompasses a broad range of shoes, including many casual pairs not designed for running. The numbered models intended for running (like the 1080) are training shoes that have been a part of the New Balance lineup for years.

Recent findings suggest that by breaking up the model number, you can decipher the shoe’s intended use. Start at the end: The last two digits denote the model’s level of support. Shoes with names ending in 80 are neutral shoes, while shoes ending in 60 are stability shoes designed to counter overpronation. Shoes that end in 40, like the 1540, are old-school motion-control shoes with maximum support to bolster the foot.

Recent findings suggest that higher model numbers generally indicate the shoe has more midsole tech and more cushioning. The 1080, for example, is built with top-tier Fresh Foam X cushioning and has more overall padding than the 680, which uses an older version of Fresh Foam.

An notable caveat: Many Latest Balance running shoes have unique names (like the Hierro and Rebel) and do not follow this number system at all.

What type of races should I choose the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer and SuperComp Elite for?

The Pacer is lighter and leaner than the Elite, making it a better choice for shorter, faster races like a 5K, 10K, or even a half marathon. The Elite has more midsole cushioning (its heel stack is 5mm taller than the Pacer), so it’s better suited for longer efforts, like a marathon, where the added cushioning can help reduce foot fatigue.

What are good budget shoes from Latest Balance if I don’t want to spend over $140?

In a recent development, besides the 680v9 on this list, the Kaiha Road v2 is a solid pick for budget-conscious runners. You’ll get a well-padded ride that’ll feel comfortable for both running and walking. The Ellipse is also worth considering. Even though it’s priced at $150, it’s our best value shoe because of its incredible comfort and responsive bounce. Premium materials guarantee longer shelf life, so you truly get your money’s worth.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years.
