Garmin LiveTrack Now Alerts Waze Drivers to Nearby Cyclists

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind.
  • Sources indicate that here’s how it works.
  • Sources indicate that waze indicates the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind. Now Garmin and Waze are flipping that warning around: Their newly introduced partnership alerts drivers when a cyclist using Garmin’s LiveTrack is nearby.

Sources indicate that here’s how it works. Start an outdoor cycling activity with LiveTrack on a compatible Garmin Edge computer or smartwatch, and your location will appear in Waze as a moving cyclist icon. Drivers don’t need to be navigating a route to see cyclists; Waze told me the icons appear whenever the app is open, as riders enter the driver’s broader route area or immediate surroundings.

Sources indicate that waze indicates the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance. In an email response to my questions, Garmin told me alerts go to “relevant drivers,” usually when the rider and driver are on the same road and traveling in the same direction. A cyclist farther ahead on the driver’s mapped route may also trigger one.

In a recent development, if several riders are together, Waze highlights one icon to avoid repeat alerts. If they spread out, multiple icons appear. Garmin describes the grouping feature as “built-in clustering logic.”.

Industry observers note that for Waze owners, cyclist alerts are on by default but can be turned off in the app’s settings. Riders opt in to Waze sharing through Garmin, but only once. After that, sharing starts whenever they begin a cycling LiveTrack, whether they start it manually or set it to start automatically.

Garmin notes any Edge computer or smartwatch with LiveTrack is compatible. LiveTrack requires a phone paired with Garmin Connect and cellular coverage; Garmin’s LTE-enabled devices can run LiveTrack without relying on the phone’s connection.

In a recent development, no additional subscription or purchase is required. Waze says drivers see only a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, not the rider’s name, identity, or exact route. Sharing stops when the ride ends.

Industry observers note that this is not V2X, the connected-vehicle technology that has been simmering in the background. V2X systems let vehicles exchange information with one another, roadside infrastructure, and other road people, including cyclists. Garmin and Waze are taking an app-based route to a similar goal: LiveTrack sends a rider’s location to Waze, which can alert drivers using the app.

Industry observers note that it’s a sensible idea, but it requires the latest apps and firmware, a Garmin rider who has opted in, a working connection, and a driver using Waze. It isn’t a substitute for cycling-friendly infrastructure, and it won’t fix distracted drivers or jerks in cars. But reminding drivers that cyclists are on the road is a step in the right direction.

Sources indicate that would you enable Waze sharing for your LiveTrack rides? If you use Waze while driving, would a cyclist icon or alert change how you approach the road? Tell us in the comments, or join me on Discord. I’d especially like to hear from riders who already use LiveTrack or Waze: What would you want to know before turning this on?

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

When I lace up for a day on the dirt, I know my trail running shoes are the only thing separating me from the rocks, roots, and miles of pure, unadulterated trail shenanigans. Trail runners, simply put, are just built different. We rack up mud and rocks with our mileage, and that means we expect more from our gear than road runners while simultaneously abusing the hell out of it. Thanks to my location on the East Coast, I get to run on a huge variety of trails, from packed singletrack to rocky technical trails, to muddy backwoods fire roads, to sandy marsh basins. Basically, I hit all the surfaces, so when I’m testing my trail shoes, I’m really digging in, and so is our legion of shoe testers.

In a recent development, this year has been an interesting year for trail running shoes. Thanks to the growing popularity of trail running, there are more coming out than ever before, but because they are so specialized, reviews are generally all over the place. That’s why on this list you will see very specific workouts for every trail running shoe that we recommend. It’s also why I proposal on updating it pretty often, and hopefully expanding the list as newly introduced shoes come out and we get our wear testers running in them. The major brands we all expect to see on this list are on here: Saucony, Altra, Salomon, and the like, but choosing trail shoes is complicated and personal, so make sure you read through these reviews to determine which are the best trail running shoes for how and where you run.

For over half a century, Runner’s World has been putting shoes through their paces with staff members and our diverse group of wear testers. These are everyday runners who hit the trailhead and make their shoes work. Every shoe I ran in was put through miles of testing based on its specificity—trail, gravel, technical shoes, et cetera. We evaluate for fit, grip, comfort, responsiveness, weather adaptability, and temperature regulation.

Sources indicate that the Hoka Speedgoat 7 makes you forget the complications of the 5 and 6. They’ve nailed the fit this time with updated uppers, fresh midsole foams, and a smarter construction that finally fixes those nagging complaints about the fit and feel. This model is seriously dialed-in now, making it the perfect shoe for flying over dusty, sandy trails where you need reliable grip without the gunk.

It has been revealed that stack height bumps to 36mm heel, 29mm forefoot using supercritical EVA foam for softer landings and snappier energy return, contrasting to the 6’s firmer feel. A winged heel counter and refined jacquard mesh upper with the addition of a gaiter mean these hug securely without hot spots or blisters, ditching the predecessor’s challenges.

Vibram Megagrip outsole upgrades to 5mm lugs with deeper siping and wider spacing; they shed sandy dust and rail trail grit effortlessly while biting hardpack and mild roots. No rock plate keeps it light and easy.

Testers hail the 7’s plush stability on dusty rails—lugs channel sand away for consistent traction; latest foam eats vibration from chatter without mush. Uppers breathe during hot days and lock miles better than the 6 ever did.

Wear-tester Diane Grim did note they run a bit smaller, so sizing up is recommended for many, especially those hitting long distances, but she loved the improved fit over the 6, and notes that “the lug pattern placement was awesome in gripping (trails were snow-covered and snowmobile groomed),” and she “loved how the lugs continue under the toes for pushing off grip.”.

“The Speedgoat 7 engulfs your foot, giving you the security and confidence to get the job done,” she states.

The shoe is a great upgrade for singletrack/rail trail runners craving reliability on flowing, gritty paths from our breakdown. It’s less for pure rock slams, but dusty cruisers never felt this good.

Sources indicate that salomon Pulsar Trail is a win for us for so many reasons, but the entry point of about $140 is hard to beat. It’s built for runners transitioning from roads or tackling milder trails, blending speed with everyday durability.

It has been revealed that this shoe rocks a 29mm heel stack and 23mm forefoot (6mm drop), delivering moderate cushion via TPU-based optiFoam². An Energy Blade TPU insert adds responsive pop and stability without bulk, making strides feel snappy yet protected.

In a recent development, the SensiFit upper with Quicklace locks your foot into the shoe—heel to toe—while breathable mesh keeps swamp feet at bay. The All Terrain Contagrip outsole features 4mm lugs for solid grip on dry dirt, gravel, and roots; it sheds mud decently but slips more on wet rocks.

No rock plate keeps weight low at 9.8 ounces, ideal for non-technical runs.

Wear-tester Rebecca Heflin praises the shoe’s comfort, stability, and versatility, wearing it from road to trail.

“The firmness of the sneaker keeps my foot more in place and safe,” she notes. “They took a run or two to break in but then were much more flexible. You could ‘feel’ the ground and what you were running on, but still felt comfortable.” This has largely been my experience as well. For a shoe with some heft, it’s nimble and easy to run in.

In a recent development, the Pulsar Trail has a stable ride; it’s plush underfoot and has Salomon’s signature snug fit. Road-to-trail types will love the smooth pavement transitions. It’s perfect for gravel or mixed surfaces from our earlier breakdown.

Saucony Peregrine 16 delivers aggressive trail performance with major upgrades, and a less aggressive drop for a closer-to-the-ground feel. It’s our top pick for technical runners hitting rocks, roots, and mud, thanks to the fact that it’s now softer and grippier than ever.

Stack height hits 32mm heel and 28mm forefoot, powered by more Pwrrun foam for smoother cushioning on long hauls. A Pwrrun+ sockliner is made to add another layer of cushioning and, gross enough, smell issues. But I’ve noticed it also helps protect your feet from creepy crawlies and mud incursion. A Vibram Megagrip outsole with 4mm lugs grips hard on wet rocks, loose dirt, snow, and roots. The traction is significantly improved over prior models despite shallower depth.

Wear-tester Diane Grim claims of the Peregrine 16s, “I LOVE this shoe! Right out of the box, amazing! Lastly, she noted the rock plate and cushioning protected her feet from jabs as she ran over sharp rocks.

The Peregrine 16 fits technical trail types perfectly from our breakdown: deep lugs and armor for rocky descents. The shoe is versatile for mixed or singletrack, too.

Some of our testers mentioned the fit was narrow. If you’ve got a wide foot, try before you buy. I am one of those sick, sick puppies who thinks that strapping on a pack and running 100 miles through the woods is a good time, and the On Cloudultra Pros are my fresh favorite shoe to do that in. Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

The Norda 055 is what happens when someone asks, “What if a hyper-technical trail shoe had a really good stack?” It’s an actual max-cushion mountain shoe with a 36mm stack in the heel and 30mm stack in the forefoot, so your quads get a soft landing while the rest of you commits to the descent.

The preferred shoe of ultrarunner Rachel Entrekin, the upper is woven from bio-circular Dyneema, a fiber with a strength-to-weight ratio 15 times that of steel. You can’t kill these shoes, and I know this because I’ve done my best to try. Sources indicate that this is a shoe that gets better with miles, which is rare. Not that it needs breaking in, but there’s a magic in the way the shoe relaxes. Yes, it costs $325. But it’s the long-haul, ultra-distance, “I have a spreadsheet for my aid stations” shoe. Per mile, it’s a bargain, and you can quote me on that when you explain it to whoever manages your budget.

It’s stable, explosive, and rugged. Basically the Linux kernel of footwear, but it actually looks good. (P.S. I only know what that is because my kid just explained that whole thing to me last night.).

Shop Men’s at nordarun.com | Shop Women’s at nordarun.com.

Trail shoes consist of four main parts: uppers, midsoles, outsoles, and rock plates. These components work together for protection, cushioning, traction, and durability on everything from gravel to gnarly singletrack.

According to recent reports, uppers form the breathable shell around your foot. They feature tough mesh with rubber overlays at the toes and heels to fend off rocks, roots, and trail debris while staying ventilated.

Midsoles provide the cushioning core, typically using EVA foam or advanced compounds like TPU or supercritical foams. They absorb shock from uneven ground and return energy to keep your legs fresh over long miles.

Sources indicate that outsoles are the grippy foundation with lugs made from sticky rubber compounds such as Vibram Megagrip. Lug depth and pattern vary by terrain: multidirectional for mud, clustered for rocks, all designed to shed debris and last through abrasion.

Rock plates sit between midsole and outsole as thin shields of plastic, aluminum, or carbon fiber. They protect against sharp stones and roots without adding much weight or stifling flexibility. With max cushioned trail shoes, they’re not necessarily a must-have anymore, though many runners still prefer them. They don’t exist in every trail shoe, and in the case where a trail shoe may have a carbon plate, it can add protection and stability.

It has been revealed that trail shoes specialize by terrain to optimize weight, grip, and protection. Choosing the right type means less slip, less fatigue, and more fun no matter the surface.

Recent findings suggest that drop refers to the heel-to-toe height difference, ranging from 0mm (zero drop for natural foot positioning) to 15mm (higher for calf relief on roads or long efforts). Low drops (0 to 4mm) build foot strength but demand adaptation; 8 to 12mm suits most runners.

Stack height measures total midsole thickness underfoot, outsole, and footbed—usually 20 to 35mm at the heel and slightly less at the forefoot. Max stack (30mm+) offers plush protection for heavy runners or rocky miles; low stack (under 25mm) delivers precise ground feel for agile, technical runs.

Gore-Tex and similar membranes laminate into uppers to block liquid water and wind while venting sweat vapor for a little bit of breathability. They shine in rain, snow, or mud, often paired with mesh drainage ports and quick-lace systems to handle stream crossings without sogginess.

Industry observers note that I’ve scrubbed enough mud from lugs to write a whole damn article on it, because nothing tanks your trail high like dried clumps firing off mid-stride. Hit them with the hose right after runs to loosen crud and clean them off. Use an old natural bristle brush and mild soap to excavate lug crevices, then stuff with newspaper or paper towels to speed drying. Never toss in the washer; it wrecks glue and mesh. Insider hack: let the muddiest shoes that you can’t get to right away dry out and then bang off the mud. It works, I promise.

Industry observers note that the stability counterpart to the Ghost 18, the Adrenaline GTS is the shoe many of us ran in when we fell in love with running. Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Recent findings suggest that brooks wanted to change what we should expect when running in a max-cushioned trainer. “We noticed that for some people, they would start running in a neutral shoe and then their body would work extra. So the internal cost was actually increasing,” mentioned Brooks Footwear PLM and BlueLine Director Nikhil Jain.

The team set out to create a shoe that would cut that internal cost. The Glycerin Flex has a decoupled heel and Flex Zone; these components allow your foot to flex naturally instead of working against a stiff, beefy platform.

Industry observers note that “Testing the Brooks Glycerin Flex was a novel experience for me on multiple fronts,” remarked Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Not only was this the first Brooks running shoe I’ve ever run in, but it was also the first hyperflexible shoe that I have ever seen—and overall, it was a positive experience. The Glycerin Flex combines the benefits of a daily trainer that allows your feet to work and get stronger with the comfort and protection of a maximalist shoe.”.

Industry observers note that we like the Glycerin Max 2 for run/walking and recovery days. The shoe has 45 mm of DNA Tuned foam in the heel and a 6 mm offset. #33912. 5 Wellness Trends We’d Like to See Go Away

5 Wellness Trends We’d Like to See Go Away

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that let’s talk about wellness trends.
  • We’re all in bodies that are designed to decay, with minds that tend to run amok and emotions that can seem like that have brains of their own.
  • Industry observers note that routines that can support your physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” Many of these approaches include habits that support your life and health—those that truly make you feel good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that let’s talk about wellness trends. More specifically, let’s talk about our collective penchant for “optimizing” the human experience.

Being a person is not always easy. We’re all in bodies that are designed to decay, with minds that tend to run amok and emotions that can seem like that have brains of their own. It’s only natural to try to control what we can—and self-care provides what can seem like an ideal platform for the pursuit.

Industry observers note that routines that can support your physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” Many of these approaches include habits that support your life and health—those that truly make you feel good. Unfortunately, many wellness trends begin in a beneficial place and spiral out of control from there.

A growing corner of self-care tends to be overly focused on tracking, streamlining, and pushing extremes. Any wellness trends that make you feel inadequate or anxious (like the examples listed below), are the ones we’d love to fade into the background.

Take what, if anything, really works for you from the below trends and then notice when it’s time to let it go.

The concept of “sleepmaxxing,” or maximizing the quality of your sleep, began swirling around social media a couple of years ago. Sleeping better is a trend we can get behind—but you don’t need expensive gadgets or high levels of anxiety to do it. More importantly, putting too much focus on your sleep habits has the potential to backfire, transforming a restful part of your day into a stressful one.

Sources indicate that good sleep is essential. Nicole Moshfegh, MD, clinical psychologist and author of The Book of Sleep, notes that proper (or inadequate) rest can affect your physical health and cognitive function, not to mention your mood. Sleep is meant to be restful. Relaxing. Restorative.

According to recent reports, your sleep routine should not be causing you additional stress. If habits like evening restorative yoga, breathwork, or less blue light after dark improve your sleep quality, maxx on! But should you find yourself agonizing over a sleep score or lying awake calculating how many minutes of rest you’re losing—both examples of orthosomnia—know that you’ve lost the plot.

According to recent reports, dunking your body into cold water might sound refreshing—and for some of the population, it is! Cold plunging is a Nordic tradition that boosts mental clarity and resilience (again, you are willingly submerging yourself in cold water) and is thought to reduce post-workout muscle stiffness, fatigue, and more.

Still, you may want to pause before adopting the cold plunge as your newly introduced cure-all. One study suggests that using cold baths for muscle recovery may be more of a placebo effect than anything else, as parsed by writer Alex Hutchinson. And for those in female bodies, further research has shown that over time, exposure to cold water can adversely effect the reproductive system, and there is no proven boon to female muscle recovery.

Between phone apps, smart watches, and bluetooth-connected rings, it’s never been easier to know exactly what’s going on in your body, at least on a biological level.

Certain smart gadgets, like the Pulse Mindfulness Ring, can act as a little buddy, helping you breathe deeply, commit to daily meditation, and focus. And when used correctly, the Oura Ring can also be a mindful companion.

Sources indicate that the glitch isn’t the tracking devices themselves, but how they’re being used. Just as putting too much stock in sleep scores can be considered an obsessive condition (again, orthosomnia), too much preoccupation with the information provided by wearable devices is proven to negatively impact psychological well-being. For some—including those with eating or health disorders—this sort of constant tracking can serve as a trigger, increasing rigidity and anxiety around otherwise healthy habits.

In short, try taking your smart accessories off sometimes, just to see how you feel.

It has been revealed that we live in a world where the breaking news about what’s going on in our minds and bodies—and, usually, what we’re lacking—is practically non-stop. And usually, there’s a supplement for that. According to one report, the global supplement market is projected to be worth $300 billion by 2028. So…ya.

Supplementing becomes an issue when you’re adding to your stack before looking to your diet and other habits. Studies have shown that supplements and weight loss pills offer a perceived sense of invulnerability, ironically leading to poorer choices in nutrition and fitness habits.

Industry observers note that another more obvious issue is supplements offered with no scientific evidence to back up purported benefits. Fast-moving digital culture and lack of oversight means that brands can pretty much say whatever they want to, which is a good thing to remember before putting anything in your body.

If your supplements are thoughtfully chosen and supplementing an existing healthy lifestyle, you’re probably on the positive side of this trend.

The internet can make your life feel like a reality show. And if you make your living as an influencer, maybe it sort of is. But even with audience perception, brand deals, and showmanship at stake, your health and wellness routine can and should make you feel good.

At its core, self-care is for you. If sharing your journey feels beneficial for you and for them, go ahead. But when your wellness practices become more about the performance of tending to yourself and less about actually doing things that bring you peace and healing, you may want to reconsider your approach.

#33910. Latest Update: Is Your AI Strength Proposal Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1351 w)

Latest Update: Is Your AI Strength Proposal Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.
  • Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.
  • We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day strategy complete with sets and reps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete).

It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.

Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.

We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day strategy complete with sets and reps.

Day one covered the lower body and core: squats or goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, reverse lunges, standing calf raises, dead bugs, and side planks.

Day two went after the upper body and posterior chain: dumbbell bench press or push-ups, rows, lat pulldowns or assisted pull-ups, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges or hip thrusts, and Pallof presses. The prescription included three sets of 8-10 reps, for 40 to 50 minutes per session, to be followed for 8-12 weeks.

It all looked perfectly sensible and not too dissimilar to what many triathletes do in most strength workouts. But for a triathlete who’s already squeezing three sports into one week, strength workouts should really be periodized and designed to augment what’s happening in the triathlete’s sport-specific training life (and the off-season is the one time of year when it’s great to do more in the gym, not less).

So with this in mind, we handed the proposal to strength coach Sam Hengehold, who works with triathletes of all ages and abilities at Kinesis Integrated Performance in Boulder, Colorado. “I’d argue it is not right, but it’s also not wrong,” she notes. “The plan is general, but it is not beneficial.”.

Here’s the surprise: Hengehold wouldn’t strike a single exercise from the list.

“All exercises listed are actually great and could very well be integrated into a triathlete strength routine,” she notes. “The limiter here is the lack of periodization and volume/load variables.”.

Two of ChatGPT’s picks earn special praise:.

In a recent development, calf raises: “Many triathletes miss this integral exercise in their strength routine,” Hengehold claims. “Lower leg injuries are extremely common with triathletes.” As a general rule, Hengehold wants athletes working toward calf raises at 1.5 times their body weight to build resiliency against injury in the calf, ankle, and foot.

Glute bridges: “A safe way to build power for beginners in strength training,” Hengehold indicates. They mostly train the glutes and core, the muscle groups that underpin all three disciplines.

It has been revealed that so if the exercises are fine, where does the wasted time come in? It’s in how the plan asks you to do them.

According to recent reports, to its credit, ChatGPT suggests lifting less often as race day approaches and adding a little load once the sets feel solid. But the exercises, sets, and reps never change. Your swim, bike, and run training is built in cycles around your races, and Hengehold advises that your lifting should be too.

In a recent development, in the off-season, strength work can take priority and endurance training becomes the base. In race season, that flips: Lifting is there to support your swim, bike, and run, and to keep your body resilient. A initiative that looks identical in January and July does neither job well.

“Over time, it will just be an energy suck of a session, causing more fatigue in the athlete with minimal benefit,” Hengehold warns.

It has been revealed that chatGPT’s warm-up gets one line: 5-10 minutes of easy cardio, mobility, and lighter practice sets. Hengehold wants something more deliberate, with activation work chosen to prepare you for the main lift of the day.

“Warm-up and activation encourages proper form and oils the muscles,” Hengehold says. “Typically, that would include some sort of dynamic stretching, mobility, or preparation exercise that will aid in the main lift goals of the session. Before squats, for example, that might mean 90/90 hip rotations for hip mobility and banded clamshells to wake up the gluteus medius.” This matters if you want to avoid injury and get the most from every rep.

In a recent development, the big, complex lifts belong at the start of the session, when you’re fresh and can control your form. They also work better when paired with an athletic movement, Hengehold states, so the brain learns what the strength is for.

According to recent reports, follow loaded squats with box jumps, for instance, and you reinforce the power you need at toe-off on the run or when pushing watts on the bike. ChatGPT’s strategy has no jumps and no explosive work at all.

In a recent development, “Neuromuscular understanding and adaptation is absolutely necessary for triathletes to maximize the benefit of strength training,” Hengehold states. Without it, you get some injury prevention and extra muscle mass, but not much else.

Hengehold named three categories of strength work that matter most for triathletes:.

Recent findings suggest that core work: Think isometric holds and slow, controlled movements, with deep breathing throughout, to work the transverse abdominal muscles. Hengehold’s picks: planks with alternating shoulder taps, dead bugs, and bird dogs.

Sources indicate that unilateral movements: Single-leg Romanian deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats, front-foot elevated reverse lunges, and single-leg calf raises all make each side do its own share of the work. Swimming, biking, and running give a stronger side plenty of chances to cover for a weaker one, and these exercises help break those overcompensation patterns.

Squat variations: Isometric squats (holding the position) and eccentric squats (slowing the lowering phase) are a safe way to build resilience in the lower body and core. The squat is also endlessly adjustable, so it can be tweaked to target whatever you need most.

What you lift, and how, should depend on how far you are from your next race.

Far from race day: This is the time for heavy strength training alongside base swim, bike, and run work. Make complex lifts the centerpiece. Hengehold likes the trap bar deadlift. Get the form and technique down first, then spend a block (typically four to six weeks) building a base with high reps and low weight. Take a deload week, then switch to low reps and heavy weight to build real strength and durability.

In race season: Triathlon training takes over, and strength work drops to maintenance. Unilateral exercises move to the front, scheduled closely around your key sessions and races. Reps and load should go mostly on perceived effort and how you’re feeling, physically and emotionally. Hengehold also stresses mobility work, foam rolling, and stretching during this period.

It has been revealed that one last thing no chatbot can do is look at your form. If you’re latest to the weight room, Hengehold recommends having a gym friend or personal trainer check your technique early on: “Bad habits are hard to break and cause damage over time, and the same is true with your swimming, biking, and running.”.

Yet technique is only part of what a generic plan misses.

It has been revealed that “Triathletes are some of the most hardworking individuals on the planet and managing training, fatigue, and recovery requires extreme attention to detail,” Hengehold says. “The time, energy, and hard work need to be maximized to be worth it, which means a generalized strength plan will not meet the standard. Each athlete is a unique individual with individual needs that require an individualized plan.”.

In a recent development, none of this is an argument against strength training — far from it. Hengehold calls it “absolutely essential to longevity in sport and health” and recommends it for every athlete. The argument is against spending your limited time and energy on a proposal that wasn’t written with you in mind.

Hot chocolate, coffee, tea, or Skratch Labs’ apple cider will warm your soul and lift your mood. And nothing hits better than a coffee stop in the middle of a cold winter ride, especially when conditions are dreary or sloppy.

Stainless insulated bottles broke into cycling about five years ago and have since exploded in popularity. They’re a proven way to keep water and hydration mix cool on the hottest summer days, and they can also keep hot drinks warm for many miles on winter rides.

Sources indicate that the Bivo Trio Bottle, available in raw stainless steel and silicone-covered stainless steel versions, has become a bottle of choice on cold-weather rides. Read on to find out why, plus tips to prevent your bottles from freezing this winter.

FULL COLD WEATHER BOTTLE TEST RESULTS.

It has been revealed that cyclists have many different methods (often handed down from one generation of riders to the next) to help prevent frozen bottles. One simple solution is to start your ride with hot water. However, depending on the temperature and ride length, this can also freeze.

It has been revealed that using insulated plastic bottles, adding a high-sodium drink mix, and wearing a hydration pack or vest under a riding jacket are all tricks I’ve used (with varying degrees of success) to keep my bottles from freezing. And some riders still swear by adding a shot of booze to their bidon. However, while these methods may prevent icing, they still result in a cold beverage during your ride.

It’s hard to miss the growing popularity of stainless steel water bottles in cycling. Their use has boomed in the last few seasons as more riders have become concerned about microplastic contamination. Plus, these metal bidons, particularly the Bivo bottles, are in the cages of many cycling influencers.

Recent findings suggest that stainless bottles typically feature a vacuum-sealed double-wall design with a coated outer and a bare stainless inner layer. Since metal bottles are rigid, you cannot squeeze them like plastic bottles. (It takes some getting used to if you haven’t ridden them before.) And while stainless bottles are much heavier than plastic models, they are heavy-duty and almost indestructible—they dent and scratch but rarely break.

Bivo is the trend-setting stainless option and commonly available from retailers like REI, Backcountry, Amazon, or your local bike shop. The Insulated Mini we tested is 17 ounces and costs $44, or opt for the 21-ounce model for $5 more.

It has been revealed that I have ridden with insulated bottles at several points in my cycling life. But until last summer, I usually stuck with non-insulated plastic bottles for most of my rides, regardless of air temperature.

Generally, I prefer the feel of a regular bottle; 22-ounce Specialized Purist bottles are my go-to, and I occasionally carry a 10-ounce Purist Maker mug for a mid-ride coffee break. But I often skip stainless insulated bottles because they aren’t squeezable and weigh noticeably more than plastic bidons.

According to recent reports, however, before a recent ride on a cold and blustery day, I filled an insulated bottle with hot chocolate and was pleased to have a warm treat throughout my 90-minute ride. So, like my insulated bottle test last summer, I applied a little science to see which insulated stainless bottles performed best in cold temps.

In a recent development, for this test, I gathered several popular metal insulated bottles. First, I evaluated the bottles by measuring water temperature over three hours in subfreezing conditions. Then, I used them on rides in cold weather to determine which worked best from a functional perspective.

While the intent was somewhat scientific, I also strove to be practical—these are tests anyone can do at home. This testing was not performed in a controlled environment or with professional-level, calibrated equipment.

In a recent development, since it was below 32 degrees outside, I was able to perform outdoor freeze testing. Like my summer insulated bottle tests, I filled the selected bottles with 400 grams of tap water (heated to 212 degrees for this test instead of chilled water used in summer). Then I placed the filled bottles on my front porch in subfreezing temperatures; I did this after sunset so sunlight would not warm the bottles. Every 30 minutes, I checked and recorded the water temperature of each bottle, in the same order each time, with a digital food thermometer.

Following the initial three-hour test period, the bottles remained overnight in sub-freezing temperatures for an additional nine hours. This tested whether the contents would stay warm for a full 12 hours (as per some bottle makers’ claims). Additionally, for reference, I subjected a Purist Maker tumbler (with 200 grams of water), an insulated plastic bottle, and a standard plastic bottle to the same tests.

The following day, I evaluated the bottles’ on-bike performance on a short loop in my neighborhood. I tested their use with standard and lobster-claw gloves (such as holding, opening caps, removing them from cages) and their nozzles’ function while drinking hot coffee (a medium-roast pour-over with some oat milk for my tests 😉).

Industry observers note that the results were clear: Insulated stainless bottles work very well in cold weather. They keep your beverage hot for an hour-long ride in 30-degree temps. For longer rides, your drink will experience some heat loss but will remain drinkably warm for three hours. The insulated metal bottles performed notably better than plastic bottles (insulated and non-insulated) for the full duration of the test.

In a recent development, after about three hours of exposure in the cold, the Bivo Insulated Trio Mini kept my coffee at a warm 119.8 degrees. This is only slightly below coffee expert James Hoffmann’s recommended coffee-drinking temp of 122 to 129 degrees. (Although I’m not sure Hoffmann would be pleased drinking three-hour-old brew.) In 12-hour testing, none of the metal bottles froze. Most bottles finished at room temperature after 12 hours outside in freezing temperatures.

In a recent development, on the bike, the Bivo valve works great, and the bottle texture isn’t overly slippery. The bottle shape is compatible with most cages, though it fits best in the Arundle Sport cage recommended by Bivo.

According to recent reports, nozzle Shield: Look for bottles with a cap that protects the nozzle. Typically, I’m not a fan of these shields when riding in warm weather—they flop around and get in the way when drinking. However, in the winter, caps keep road salt and slush off the bottle’s nozzle, and they also help prevent icing. Ones with a removable plastic or rubber shield are easier to clean; plus, you can use the bottles without the cap on warm days.

It has been revealed that vapor Pressure: Many of the tested bottles carry a warning about using liquids hotter than 180 degrees. This is to avoid scalding and burns from pressurized hot water when the cap or nozzle is opened. With insulated bottles, hot liquid heats the air inside the bottle enough to spray potentially near-boiling water into your mouth or onto your body.

Industry observers note that avoid this by letting your hot beverage cool slightly before pouring it into your bottle. For long rides (when using two bottles of hot drinks), save the hotter bottle for later in the day. This way, it has time to cool to a drinkable temperature.

Cage Compatibility: Since they do not deform or flex, metal bottles don’t pair with every bottle cage. Some stainless bottles have a loose fit in cages (bottles can even eject on rough roads), and some cage shapes do not allow some metal bottles to sit correctly, causing annoying rattling and buzzing while riding. Other cage-bottle pairings are so tight that it’s hard to remove the bottle while riding.

My advice: Check that your cages work before dropping up to $100 for new bottles that won’t fit. Some brands have specific cage recommendations on their sites. You can also read user reviews for the compatibility of different bottles and cages. Also, be sure to check the overall bottle height to be sure it fits in your frame.

Dropped Bottles: I do not recommend using metal bottles in mass-start situations; use plastic bidons for substantial group rides or races. When a metal bottle is ejected from a cage on a bump, or you drop one (as is prone to happen with cold hands or when wearing bulky gloves), it ricochets off the road surface more than a plastic bottle. And while metal makes these bottles more durable, they do not burst open on impact or crush if hit by other riders.

According to recent reports, bivo shook up the bottle market when it debuted its stainless steel bottles. The small Richmond, Vermont-based company launched insulated bottles shortly after, and cyclists have fallen in love with them. They work well, look good, and don’t have a funky taste.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Newly introduced England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Physical Therapists Share the Most Effective QL Stretches and Exercises for Runners With Lower Back and Hip Pain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that most runners are familiar with the significant muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes.
  • A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World.
  • When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that most runners are familiar with the significant muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still vital—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.

A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.

When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.

If this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew claims. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.

It has been revealed that there are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a major, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.

Industry observers note that another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

In a recent development, yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can concerns in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas says.

Sources indicate that keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas states. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”.

Recent findings suggest that A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great challenges if left unchecked. A substantial one? Compromised running mechanics.

Industry observers note that A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew indicates. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

On top of that, a tight QL can also hinder your breathing. As mentioned above, one of the QL’s jobs is to help you inhale, so when this muscle is tight, you may not be able to breathe as deeply or easily, Agnew says.

It has been revealed that plagued by what you think may be an irritated QL? Try Agnew’s three-step at-home series to help reduce your discomfort.

Perform this sequence as often as every day if you’re in significant discomfort that’s limiting your ability to run. In the case of minor pain, incorporate this series two to three times per week. On the days you run, perform the myofascial release, pelvic tilts, and hip hikes before you lace up, then tackle the other components afterward.

This can help turn down the pain response in a barking QL by desensitizing soft tissue, Agnew explains.

How to Perform Myofascial Release.

Sources indicate that the pelvic tilts help you learn how to coordinate and control pelvic motion so you can maintain proper mechanics while running, and the hip hikes help activate your QL. The kettlebell side bend increases blood flow to the muscle, which can aid in healing. Finally, the suitcase carry increases strength, stability, and engagement of the muscle, which can ensure it functions properly during a run.

Lengthen your QL—as well as tight hip flexors—with this two-for-one half-kneeling lunge stretch.

Industry observers note that do these moves daily or several times per day to mobilize your lower back. Perform them before or after a run. Crucial caveat: If your QL hurts more after stretching—or if your QL pain returns soon after stretching—then stretches are likely not the solution and you should stop doing them, Haas explains.

Dynamic QL Mobility + Hip 90/90.

Recent findings suggest that to start, do one set of these moves daily to help your body learn the neuromuscular patterns. (The caveat: If you feel sore, then skip a day.) After about six weeks, do these moves two to three times per week as part of your regular strength-training routine.

Recent findings suggest that this exercise targets the glutes and works on pelvic control in a movement pattern that’s similar to running. Think of it as an opportunity to train proper glute use in your running form, which will help unload any strain on your QL caused by weak glutes.

Recent findings suggest that this exercise can improve core stability and strengthen the glutes, resulting in improved running mechanics and less stress on your QL. You’ll need a long, looped resistance band.

Sources indicate that sometimes, despite your best at-home efforts to treat an irritated QL, it’s still best to get checked out by a physical therapist. Haas recommends booking a PT appointment if you try the above stretches and strength moves and don’t see improvements after about two weeks.

Recent findings suggest that agnew suggests getting evaluated by a PT if you’re in so much pain that it’s inhibiting your running. In this case, getting seen sooner can help mitigate pain before further issues arise, Agnew explains.

#33907. Breaking: How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2012 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training.
  • In a recent development, as it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike.
  • Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training. But with work and family lives, it can feel impossible to find the hours in the week to properly commit to a base build, especially if you’re a beginner cyclist who’s not used to rides that take more than three hours.

In a recent development, as it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike. Building a base of fitness for cycling takes some commitment and consistency, but it doesn’t have to take over your life.

Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.

Industry observers note that A lot of cyclists think that if they can’t train 10-plus hours per week, their fitness will suffer, or they won’t make gains on the bike. This isn’t true, especially for newer riders. “Someone who has not been doing any exercise would see gains in as little as two to four hours a week of riding,” says Brooke. “If someone has some general fitness, gains could be had in four to six hours [per week].”.

However, expect that after a few weeks or months, the tangible signs of progress will slow unless you can devote more time to training. “The tricky part is the ongoing gains might not be as easy to see as the initial gains,” Brooke adds. “Initially, if the athlete was measuring power, they would see power increases, but these would plateau in a few months, leading them to think gains are no longer occurring but in reality, the athlete is likely to still build other metrics of fitness like repeatability, durability, and resilience, but those are not as easy to measure.”.

Often, upcoming cyclists with limited time tend to attempt one monster ride on the weekend, skipping cycling during the week due to busy lives. But even if you can only eke out two one-hour (or 45-minute!) trainer sessions on weekdays in addition to the long weekend ride, you’ll gain fitness and strength faster than if you stick to a single ride.

“I would rather see the athlete do three quality days a week versus one or even two longer days,” says Brooke.

“The base training goal, whether you’re a pro or average Joe, is to build the best aerobic fitness you can for the training hours you have available,” indicates Brooke. Without this aerobic fitness, you won’t be able to boost your speed or power on the bike.

Industry observers note that this means spending the bulk of your time on the bike in zone 2 (whether you use power, heart rate or perceived exertion). Riding in zone 2—also known as your endurance pace—will mean that you’re able to hold a conversation and speak in full sentences, but it should feel slightly difficult to do so. If you can chat away easily, you’re riding a little too easy. If you’re gasping for air between sentences, you’re riding a little too hard.

By that, we mean your skin. Riding more miles means being aware of skin considerations such as sun protection and chafing prevention. Don’t just ignore reddened skin, use lubricants and padded shorts to feel more comfortable on the bike.

In a recent development, for newer riders, opt for the longer durations in each phase. If you’ve been riding for a while, you’ll likely notice that after a few weeks in each phase, you’re at a point where you’re not noticing any improvements—in that case, proceed to the next phase. Here’s how Brooke would break it down.

2.5-3.5 hours (zone 2), based on how much free time you have available.

New riders may need to break up the zone 3 portion of the ride with an easy 5-10 minutes in the middle.

2.5-4 hour (zone 2) based on how much free time you have available.

Have an extra hour on Saturday for your long ride? Great! Woke up an hour early on Wednesday and have time to hop on the trainer for an extra 45-minute ride in zone 2? Fantastic. Feel free to add time whenever possible.

Sources indicate that four days on the bike is better than three, claims Brooke. “Two harder interval days and two longer days would be best if possible,” she notes. And this is actually a fairly standard schedule for most serious cyclists—they’ll add one or two additional easy rides to the schedule, but the meat and potatoes of their training consists of two longer endurance rides and two harder interval-based sessions.

It has been revealed that in fact, Brooke says that often, she hears new cyclists say they only have four hours per week to train, but once they get going, they start to “find” extra time. “You would be surprised how many newer riders think they are limited to four to six hours a week but once they really get into cycling, they make accommodations to squeeze in an extra hour or two per week,” she says. “I see riders all the time start to wake up earlier to squeeze in additional ride time before they start the rest of the day!”.

Recent findings suggest that and thanks to the prevalence of indoor trainers, it’s easier than ever to sneak in an extra hour or two on the bike during a weekend or early in the morning, even if you have work or childcare demands on your time. But don’t neglect outdoor riding, especially if your base-building goal is to be able to keep up on the local group ride or jump into a race. While indoor training builds fitness, it doesn’t help improve your skills for riding outdoors, so make time for at least one outdoor ride per week if at all possible.

Sources indicate that there is one final caveat: It’s easy to get excited about the prospect of adding a monster ride to your weekend whenever possible, but these long rides aren’t easy. Four hours on the bike will feel very, very different from two hours. If riding for five hours on Saturday means you can barely walk for two days after, or it impacts your training the next week, back off.

It has been revealed that long rides shouldn’t leave you flattened for days afterwards. If they do, you’re doing too much, too soon. And Brooke notes that the longer you ride, the more important it is to properly fuel that long effort!

The fastest way to improve your fitness is—again—by consistently training. But training doesn’t mean all-bike-all-the-time! Brooke indicates there are quite a few simple additions you can do on those non-cycling days to see gains on the bike.

Recent findings suggest that → Walk: Often on conference calls for work, or accompanying your kiddos to soccer practice? Walk and talk, or do laps around the field while you cheer. “Walking is more of an aerobic builder than people think and can be a gentle form of aerobic activity to accompany bike time,” Brooke claims.

For the office worker, treadmill desks are becoming more popular, and if you do want to put in more bike time and you have a stationary trainer, you can do some easy spinning while answering emails or brainstorming for that big presentation.

→ Strength Train: “Strength training can be added in as little as 15 minutes a day, three days a week if we are willing to change the paradigm of going to the gym and lifting heavy things,” claims Brooke. “Integrating just this small amount of functional strength into a base training program like we do at BaseCamp yields long-term benefits to your training and health.”.

You can do shortstrength sessions at home with just a couple of weights, or even bodyweight alone to get started.

In a typical training initiative, cyclists have three weeks of training followed by a rest week where they do only a couple of shorter, easier rides. When you’re only able to ride three days a week, there’s no reason to take a rest week—you’re already getting plenty of recovery time in the four days you’re off the bike.

Sources indicate that “The low training stimulus is likely not enough to elicit a high enough super-compensation response to make the loss of fitness during a rest week worth it,” claims Brooke. (That said, if you’re a beginner rider and find that after three weeks, you are feeling fatigued, you can dial down the duration or intensity for that fourth week—but stick to three rides if possible.).

Industry observers note that once you’ve done your base training for several weeks with your rides spread out through the week (i.e Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday), you may want to try switching things up. If you do have the ability to try out upcoming riding days, it’s worth experimenting with doing mini-training blocks, i.e riding three days in a row, some weeks. This subtle shift changes your training stimulus by forcing your body to contend with the need for speedier recovery between rides.

Newer riders may find that it’s harder to recover between rides in these chunks, indicates Brooke. “The challenge of block training is the athlete needs a certain amount of base fitness to be able to respond and adapt to this type of stimuli and in this scenario,” she explains. “But testing the block process is the only way to find out how they tolerate it.”.

If you try riding three days in a row and feel exhausted, go back to your regular schedule and test again after another few weeks of consistent training.

Industry observers note that while it’s tempting to stay in the base phase forever, this training phase should really only last around eight weeks. At this point, your aerobic fitness is maximized (for now) and it’s time to focus on the development of “power.”.

In a recent development, “After the base phase comes the build phase, where the athlete wants to increase their sustainable max power for a range of times,” indicates Brooke. “For a newer cyclist without a specific goal, focus on holding a higher wattage for five minutes to 40 minutes. This phase should be maintained as long as the athlete continues to see improvement, then once response begins to fade, move on to the next phases.”.

Once you’ve plateaued your power gains, the final phase, typically utilized when “peaking” for an event would be the “speed” phase, explains Brooke. “Here, the cyclist would focus on improving shorter efforts of under five minutes and building anaerobic capacity to focus on performing better in events or group rides.”.

After your main event, whether it’s a race or group ride or even just spending four to six weeks focusing on upping your sprint power, it’s time to take a short break and then circle back to base phase.

The good news is that once you’ve completed this cycle, you’ll be pleasantly surprised at how much stronger you’re feeling on the bike the second time you tackle base training. While training phases are cyclical, your fitness grows as you spend more and more time on the bike, so no training phase will feel exactly the same.

Molly writes about cycling, nutrition and training with an emphasis on bringing more women into sport. She co-hosts The Consummate Athlete Podcast and spends most of her free time biking and running on trails, occasionally joined by her mini-dachshund.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past problems beginning in 1975. This article about restorative yoga for stress relief first appeared in the September-October 1995 problem of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Anthropologists tell us that our bodies have not changed much over our millions of years of being human. Our ancestors had the same anatomical and physiological characteristics as contemporary men and women who drive freeways and communicate via the information superhighway. We have an ancient body subjected to a modern problem: living with chronic stress.

It has been revealed that at one time, stress was a term used chiefly by physiologists who measured its effects in their laboratories. Today the term is used in common parlance. “I’m stressed out” is a familiar idiom describing how a life lived on overload affects health, sexual function and reproduction, relationships, job performance, athletic performance, and, most key, one’s sense of self. The effects of stress have reached epidemic proportions in our lives, and stress-related diseases have become a medical specialty.

Industry observers note that sometimes the effects of stress present themselves during milestone life events: marriage, the birth of a child, getting a upcoming job, or the death of a loved one. Other times it’s the little things that get us as we try to juggle the myriad responsibilities of job and family. Regardless of the trigger, stress is often accompanied by one or more negative effects—impatience, frustration, irritation, anger, muscle tension, headache, indigestion, or poor elimination. One thing is certain: The more stress we experience, the more its effects compound within us. When stress becomes chronic, it can lead to disease.

Stress begins with a physiological response to what your body-mind perceives as life-threatening. For our ancestors, this may have been defending against the aggression of a hungry animal. For modern-day humans, this may be living with the fear of losing a job in a sagging economy or the health crisis of a family member.

Whatever the stressor, the mind alerts the body that danger is present. In response, the adrenal glands, located above the kidneys, secrete catecholamine hormones. These adrenaline and noradrenalin hormones act upon the autonomic nervous system, as the body prepares for fight or flight. Heart rate, blood pressure, mental alertness, and muscle tension are increased. The adrenal hormones cause metabolic changes that make energy stores available to each cell and the body begins to sweat. The body also shuts down systems that are not a priority in the immediacy of the moment, including digestion, elimination, growth, repair, and reproduction.

Sources indicate that these adaptive responses have been positive for the survival of the human race over thousands of years. For our ancestors, a stressful situation usually resolved itself quickly. They fought or they ran, and, if they survived, everything returned to normal. The hormones were used beneficially, the adrenal glands stopped producing stress hormones, and systems that were temporarily shut down resumed operation.

According to recent reports, to our detriment, modern men and women are often unable to resolve stress so directly, and live lives chronically stressed as a result. Still responding to the fight-or-flight response, the adrenals continue to pump stress hormones. The body does not benefit from nutrition because the digestion and elimination systems are slowed down. Even sleep is disturbed by this agitated state.

In a chronically stressed state, quality of life, and perhaps life itself, is at risk. The body’s capacity to heal itself is compromised, either inhibiting recovery from an existing illness or injury, or creating a latest one, including high blood pressure, ulcers, back pain, immune dysfunction, reproductive problems, and depression. These conditions add stress of their own, and the cycle continues.

The antidote to stress is relaxation. To relax is to rest deeply. Relaxation is a state in which there is no movement, no effort, and the brain is quiet.

Recent findings suggest that common to all stress reduction techniques is putting the body in a comfortable position, with gentle attention directed toward the breath. Do these techniques really work? Scientists have researched the effects of relaxation and report measurable benefits, including reduction in muscle tension and improved circulation.

Sources indicate that among the first to study relaxation was Edmund Jacobson, M.D. In 1934, he wrote You Must Relax, a book about the benefits of his progressive relaxation techniques. He reported success in using his approach to treat high blood pressure, indigestion, colitis, insomnia, and what he called “nervousness.”.

One of the foremost writers and researchers in the field of stress reduction today is Herbert Benson, M.D., who coined the phrase “relaxation response” to describe the physiological and mental responses that occur when one consciously relaxes. In The Wellness Book he defines the relaxation response as “a physiological state characterized by a slower heart rate, metabolism, rate of breathing, lower blood pressure, and slower brain wave patterns.”.

Recent findings suggest that david Spiegel, M.D., author of Living Beyond Limits, reports, “In medicine, we are learning that physical problems such as high blood pressure and heart disease can be influenced by psychological interventions such as relaxation training. Indeed, the Food and Drug Administration issued a report recommending these non-drug approaches as the treatment of choice for milder forms of hypertension. Mind and body are connected and must work together, and this should be a powerful asset in treating medical illness.”.

Sources indicate that indeed, body and mind are connected. Relatively new in medicine is the specialty called psychoneuroimmunology, another way of saying that body and mind—or psyche, nervous system, and immune system—are connected. This specialty understands that the health of the psyche is reflected in, and partly created by, the health of the body, and vice versa.

Industry observers note that among those whose scientific study supports the body-mind connection is Dean Ornish, M.D., author of Dr. Dean Ornish’s Program for Reversing Heart Disease. He studied those with atherosclerotic heart disease and concluded that daily periods of relaxation are essential in preventing further deterioration.

Sources indicate that I often refer to restorative yoga poses as “active relaxation.” By supporting the body with props, we alternately stimulate and relax the body to move toward balance. Some poses have an overall benefit. Others target an individual part. All create specific physiological responses which are beneficial to health and can reduce the effects of stress-related disease.

Restorative poses help relieve the effects of chronic stress in several ways. First, the use of props provides a completely supportive environment for total relaxation.

Second, each carefully designed restorative sequence moves the spine in all directions. These movements illustrate the age-old wisdom of yoga, which teaches that well-being is enhanced by a healthy spine. Some of the restorative poses are backbends, while others are forward bends. Additional poses gently twist the column both left and right.

Sources indicate that third, a well-sequenced restorative practice also includes an inverted pose, which reverses the effects of gravity. This can be as simple as putting the legs on a bolster or pillow, but the effects are quite dramatic. Because we stand or sit most of the day, blood and lymph fluid accumulate in the lower extremities. By changing the relationship of the legs to gravity, fluids are returned to the upper body and heart function is enhanced.

Psychobiologist and yoga teacher Roger Cole, Ph.D., consultant to the University of California, San Diego, in sleep research and biological rhythms, has done preliminary research on the effects of inverted poses. He found that they dramatically alter hormone levels, thus reducing brain arousal, blood pressure, and fluid retention. He attributes these benefits to a slowing of heart rate and dilation of the blood vessels in the upper body due to reversing the effects of gravity.

Finally, yoga teaches that the body is permeated with energy. Prana, the masculine energy, resides above the diaphragm, moves upward, and controls respiration and heart rate. Apana, the feminine energy, resides below the diaphragm, moves downward, and controls the function of the abdominal organs. Restorative yoga balances these two aspects of energy so that the practitioner is neither overstimulated nor depleted.

In general, restorative poses are for those times when you feel weak, fatigued, or stressed from your daily activities. They are especially beneficial for the times before, during, and after major life events: the death of a loved one, change of job or residence, marriage, divorce, major holidays, and vacations. In addition, you can practice the poses when ill or recovering from illness or injury.

The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a fresh study on anti-movement vs.
  • “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

Recent findings suggest that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a fresh study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

“Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

According to recent reports, when we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

According to recent reports, why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly key for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

According to recent reports, when running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

While running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

In a recent development, while some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

In a recent development, enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an vital role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

Sources indicate that runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.
