Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

One helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Sources indicate that through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

Runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

At the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

For runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Before the Adrenaline GTS debuted in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

In 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Sources indicate that now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Guide rails offer unobtrusive support for both overpronators and neutral runners.

Our lab tests show that DNA Loft remains Brooks’s softest midsole material.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

The most responsive expression of Brooks’s DNA foam debuted on the Hyperion Tempo.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

Sources indicate that we always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

It has been revealed that according to testers, the Hyperion Elite 6 feels less softer and more accommodating compared to other super shoes they’ve tested. The newly introduced DNA Gold midsole adds more edge compared to the Hyperion Elite’s DNA Flash foams, with testers saying the rebound is comparable to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5.

Does Brooks have bargain-priced shoes and how do they stack up to more expensive models?

According to recent reports, the Launch 12, included on this list, has a fit and feel almost on par with more expensive models. It’s not as responsive compared to $140 to $160 trainers due to its EVA cushioning, but it delivers a smooth ride.

Sources indicate that amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

These Three Offseason Strength Exercises Can Help You Break Through Your Climbing Plateau

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time.
  • According to recent reports, for a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside.
  • The workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time. If you’re thinking about winterizing your bike for the season, then it’s the perfect time to start looking at your strength training plan for the offseason.

According to recent reports, for a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside. For others it takes form as time on fat bikes, skis, or even a pair of running shoes. Regardless of how your winter activities take shape, be sure to add some strength training to make sure you can hit your 2027 goals.

The workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training. Each exercise targets a different part of the body to dial in the strength you need when you are trying to power up climbs next year. The workout can be done as a stand-alone set of exercises or it can be added on to your current strength training plan.

Sources indicate that so many cyclists want to just spend time in the saddle for training—that’s great up to a point. Eventually we all need to get off the bike and spend some time strength training to help break through those frustrating plateaus. These three overlooked exercises can help you elevate your climbs for 2027.

Today I had my first hill-focused ride after a few weeks focusing on running and trainer rides. The first steep pitch swiftly reminded me how much I use my upper body while getting up a hill on the bike. As I climbed, I felt myself pulling on the handlebar with each pedal stroke while gravity was trying to pull me back. Developing the pull muscles is something that will benefit the whole kinetic chain while climbing. Bent-over rows in particular are a great upper-body exercise for this because they engage multiple muscle groups for one movement pattern. Rows can be done with so many different types of equipment: dumbbells, kettlebells, TRX Suspension Systems, elastic bands, and more. Here’s how I recommend doing them with dumbbells.

One of the reasons I love deadlifts for cyclists is because they are exercises that works almost all the muscles through the kinetic chain in one simple move. As we climb, we are pulling energy through our upper body, driving through the hips, and pushing the power through our legs into the pedals. This exercise trains the muscles through your arms, back, and core, while simultaneously working the muscles throughout your legs. Another reason deadlifts are one of my go-to exercises is that they can be done with several different types of equipment. My favorite equipment for this exercise is a barbell, but deadlifts can be done with dumbbells and kettlebells too.

Recovery Tip: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is very real, and depending on the person, your muscle burn can last for a few days after your training session. Initiative accordingly for your rides following a heavy weight day. Listen to your body and add a recovery ride or off-bike activity if that's what you need.

Recent findings suggest that your core is what ties everything in your body together, so it is integral to grow your stability and power here. While riding today, I was trying to really be in tune with how I was using my core when climbing. When I was in the saddle I felt like the focus from my core was on stability, allowing for a sound upper body while pushing power through my legs and out of the pedals. My simple go-to core exercise to improve climbing is a plank with cross-body knee taps. This works stability through your core while working the internal obliques through the cross-body motion of the knee tuck. This exercise will really show its gains when you get out of the saddle as the climb pitches up.

Sources indicate that A quick note on consistency: strength training will give you the best results when you incorporate it in your plan week after week. It will offer significantly diminished results if you are sprinkling it in sporadically. If you are able to, try to commit to adding strength training consistently for a four- to six-week block and see how that impacts your rides.

Our strength training program can help get you started with a more in-depth workout plan. It’s key to remember it does not matter where you are in your cycling journey, there are gains to be found from adding some level of strength training to your calendar.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant.
  • Sources indicate that so when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from.
  • "I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr mentioned, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant. The two bottles bounced loosely against my chest, with water leaking down my shirt throughout the run. It was not a flattering look. Every step came with its own sloshing soundtrack. I spent so much time adjusting the thing (despite an across-the-chest strap) that I barely enjoyed my run.

Sources indicate that so when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from. During a Reddit AMA hosted by BBC Sport, the Scottish middle-distance star, who casually broke the mile world record in July with a 3:42.66 finish, shared his thoughts on the growing popularity of running vests.

"I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr mentioned, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.

For context, we're talking about a world-record holder, Olympic medalist, and world champion in the 1500 meters. He knows a thing or two about logging miles. And while 12 miles might look quite different on his watch than mine, I don't think his suggestion was particularly outrageous.

And because everything is contested on the internet, plenty of people disagree.

Runner @natalie.the.capn shared Kerr's comments on Threads and explained that she wears a hydration belt on every outing so she has somewhere to keep her phone, particularly in case of an emergency. "Funny how men rarely think of that," she wrote.

I do understand her concern. I'm a guy, so I'm definitely not going to pretend I have the same safety considerations that women often face while exercising alone. I also bring my phone everywhere, usually carrying it in my hand because iPhones only get bigger and the pockets on most of my running shorts haven't kept up.

She also pointed out that some of her routes take her six miles or more between places where she can get water, which is an entirely different experience from mine.

I live in New York City, where Central Park has plenty of water fountains (that work ... most of the time) and there's usually a deli within walking distance to snag a Gatorade. I can see why Kerr's approach makes sense here, especially for shorter runs. I've also tried handheld bottles and waist straps, and neither has been particularly enjoyable. Between the bouncing, adjusting, and occasional hand cramps, I'd love to carry as little as possible in my hands.

It has been revealed that that changes a lot during marathon training, something I've put myself through four times now, when I'm out for considerably longer and need water to wash down those pasty gels. Aside from the hydration aspect, stopping to buy something, pausing my watch, and interrupting my stride halfway through a long run is a vibe killer.

It has been revealed that and I'm certainly not arguing against being prepared. I learned the hard way that sunscreen deserved a permanent spot in my prerun routine after years of neglecting it ended with some casual skin cancer surgery.

According to recent reports, the Threads debate, naturally, has brought out some pretty different opinions. One commenter, siding with Kerr, wrote, "Yeah im gonna listen to the guy who runs for a living but thanks." Others pointed out that beginners, slower runners, and people training in hot weather could have very different hydration needs.

They're definitely right about that. Twelve miles is a long way for plenty of runners, no matter what their experience level, and access to water, weather, pace, and individual needs all change the equation. Kerr even acknowledged that people have different reasons for carrying gear, something that seems to have gotten a little lost as his comments made their way around social media.

I still think he has a fair point about how much equipment we sometimes convince ourselves we need on a run. That said, if your vest makes your runs more comfortable or gives you peace of mind, by all means wear it. For me, I'll be keeping my phone close and bringing an appropriate amount of water when I need it.

As for my hydration vest, it's been collecting dust ever since that first outing, and I haven't missed it one bit.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours.
  • Industry observers note that and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix.
  • Industry observers note that to get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours. It can show up as pain behind the knee, pressure in the saddle, numbness, or that familiar feeling that you’re reaching for the pedal instead of driving through it.

Industry observers note that and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix. Riders often blame the saddle itself, their bib shorts, or even their flexibility when the problem is simply that the seat is a little too high.

Industry observers note that to get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change. Check out Bicycling’s Guide to the Perfect Bike Fit.

That said, saddle height is also where fit advice gets messy. There isn’t one perfect number that works for everyone, and the usual rules of thumb are only starting points. Your ideal height depends on your body, your mobility, your injury history, your cleat setup, and more.

Quick Signs Your Saddle May Be Too High• Pain behind the knee • Saddle sores or numbness • Discomfort where your hamstrings meet your glutes • Rocking hips while pedaling • Reaching for the pedal at the bottom of the stroke Quick Fix• Lower the saddle a few millimeters, do a real ride, and reassess.

Here’s how to tell whether your saddle may be too high and a simple at-home check you can do before your next ride.

Saddle height is one of the first things riders adjust, and for good reason. When it’s close, you feel smoother and more comfortable. When it’s off, the problems can spread everywhere.

In a recent development, but this is where people get tripped up: saddle height is crucial, but it is only one element in an interconnected system. If your cleats are in the wrong place, your saddle is too far forward or back, or your crankarms don’t suit you, changing saddle height alone may not solve much. It’s the beginning of fit, not the whole thing.

Sources indicate that A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel. Two riders with the same height and inseam may still end up at different saddle heights because bodies aren’t identical and neither are pedaling styles.

Industry observers note that pain is the clearest warning that something in your position needs attention. Riding is hard. Suffering through an interval is one thing. Pain caused by pressure, strain, or repeated irritation from a bad setup is another.

A saddle that’s too high often shows up in a few predictable ways:.

According to recent reports, this is the classic one. If you feel pain at the back of the knee, especially after longer rides or harder efforts, a too-high saddle is one possible cause.

According to recent reports, but not the only one. Fit problems tend to overlap. So treat this as a clue, not a verdict.

If the back of your pedal stroke feels strained, tight, or tuggy, especially when you’re trying to make power, your saddle may be a little high.+.

A high saddle can make you unstable on the bike. Instead of sitting planted, you start shifting and searching. That extra motion can increase friction and pressure, which can mean hot spots, sores, and numbness.

If your hips are dropping side to side at the bottom of the pedal stroke, there’s a decent chance you’re compensating for too much saddle height.

Some riders point their toes naturally. But if you’re really reaching at the bottom of the stroke and compensating by going toes-down, that can be another sign the saddle is too high.

In a recent development, rocking hips can also happen with a saddle that’s too low. So can a toes-down pedaling style. Tight hamstrings, limited mobility, weak core stability, and other fit issues can all muddy the picture. Back-of-knee pain can come from saddle height, but it can also come from saddle fore-aft, cleat setup, or a combination of things.

In a recent development, that doesn’t make the signs worthless. It just means you should think in patterns, not absolutes.

If you have knee pain plus hip rocking plus pressure and instability in the saddle, now the case gets stronger.

Todd Carver, Specialized’s human performance manager, shared a simple check that can help flag a saddle that may be too high.

If the distance from heel to pedal is more than about one centimeter, your saddle could be too high.

The result is a prompt to look closer, not a green light to make significant changes without further investigation.

Don’t make a giant change. That’s how you turn one problem into several problems.

Recent findings suggest that start small. Lower the saddle a few millimeters at a time, then ride it long enough to notice whether the change actually helps. One short spin around the block is not enough. You want enough ride time to see whether the pain eases, whether your pedaling feels smoother, and whether you stop shifting around on the saddle.

If you’re dealing with persistent pain, don’t keep self-diagnosing forever.

A good fit pro can sort out whether saddle height is the actual problem or just the most obvious symptom.

Riders fixate on saddle height because it feels fundamental. And it is. But it’s also just one part of a system.

According to recent reports, A high saddle can absolutely cause trouble. So can cleat position. So can saddle setback. So can crank length. So can your mobility. The goal is not to chase some magic formula you found online. It’s to get to a position that lets you pedal smoothly, make power comfortably, and finish rides feeling worked, not damaged.

That’s why the best takeaway is a modest one: use the common signs, do a quick check, make small changes, and listen to what your body tells you.

In a recent development, there are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

In a recent development, keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

According to recent reports, this budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Industry observers note that using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

In a recent development, besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

Sources indicate that the bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

This is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another significant plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

To keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more.

According to recent reports, merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. It follows the familiar design cues of premium exercise bikes — a sturdy frame, heavy flywheel, and whisper-quiet belt-drive system. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

The Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. It connects via Bluetooth to the Echelon Fit app, allowing you to track speed, distance, and calories. If you’re taking a live class, you can also view your ranking on the leaderboard. The app offers over 40 live classes daily and a library of more than 15,000 on-demand sessions. While the bike doesn’t have a built-in screen, its device holder accommodates tablets up to 8 inches wide.

That noted, you don’t need the connected features to get a great workout. At its core, this is a solid, well-built exercise bike with a heavy flywheel and 32 resistance levels, manually adjusted with a knob behind the handlebar. The bike features a “one size fits most” design, with adjustable saddle and handlebar positions to suit most adults. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

Industry observers note that with Bluetooth and USB connectivity to the Schwinn ConnectTM, Zwift, and MyFitnessPal apps, this stationary bike is a great option for interactive workouts—particularly if you want to work through pre-programmed sessions and track your progress over time. The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

Industry observers note that unlike many of the bikes we've selected that adjust gradually in difficulty at the turn of a knob, this model has 25 preset levels of magnetic resistance, which provides a nice range in difficulty. The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit owners from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

Looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

Recent findings suggest that while it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

Sources indicate that people love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”.

Just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s key to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

In a recent development, for example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, says Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” states Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews.

According to recent reports, when you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

In a recent development, flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

Recent findings suggest that since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Sources indicate that fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.

Our Editors Rode Dozens of E-Bikes. These 12 Are Worth Buying for Commuting, Trails, Cargo, and Tight Budgets

📅 20 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that you wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions.
  • I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in New York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that you wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions. However, whether you’re hunting for deals or seeking out the latest tech, now is the time to buy. With holiday discounts and latest e-bikes rolling out to dealers and online retailers, plenty of great commuter, cargo, and e-MTB options are out there—at great prices.

I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in New York City. Plus, I commute daily on an e-bike and ride test dozens of electric bikes each year. Last summer, I even went almost entirely car-free thanks to an electric cargo bike.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re choosing your first e-bike, upgrading to a newer model, or adding another electric model to your garage, dozens of great options are available—and our editors and staff have tested many of them. No matter your age, cycling ability, or budget, brands offer electric bikes that meet needs.

Industry observers note that tip for E-Bike Buyers: Don’t overpay for an electric bike, but spend what you can comfortably afford. If an e-bike is fun to ride, you’ll use it more often. It’s more cost-effective to buy an e-bike equipped the way you want it upfront than to upgrade it later. Also, remember: you cannot change an electric bike’s motor system if you decide you want more power.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. Over several years, the Level platform has proven to be reliable and low-maintenance. Plus, its price doesn’t break the bank.

Aventon split the 4th-generation Level into two models. The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. Aventon also added regenerative braking, increasing the bike’s range up to 75 miles. The pricier ADV edition features a mid-drive motor; it bumps up the torque to 100 Nm and range to 110 miles. Both versions come standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

In a recent development, another feature owners will find quite useful is the Level’s connected features. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

BUY LEVEL 4 STEP-THROUGH BUY LEVEL 4 ADV.

Industry observers note that the relatively affordable seven-speed model Soltera 2.5 from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat. This makes it an excellent choice for getting around town or quick commutes. It’s even better than the original version, thanks to hydraulic disc brakes. A push of the throttle gets you started; then, the brushless hub motor gently assists your pedaling.

Recent findings suggest that along with disc brakes, the Soltera features integrated lights and turn signals, and the battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (rather than the bolt-on batteries found on many similarly-priced e-bikes). Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a strikingly light 46-pound package.

Aventon also offers a singlespeed, Soltera 3 ADV with a Gates belt-drive system.

It has been revealed that when buying a low-priced e-bike, a simple, low-cost, easy-to-repair, and reliable model usually beats out complicated designs. Lectric’s XP Lite2 is about as basic as it gets. It has a low-maintenance singlespeed drivetrain, a 300-watt hub motor, and a 375Wh battery. With its compact size, 20x2.5-inch tires, and twist-grip throttle, the XP Lite is perfect for zipping through traffic, commuting to the office, or heading to the gym or bar after work.

The XP Lite2 features only one gear and a 300W motor, so it’s not ideal for very hilly terrain. But with the throttle, you can get over small rises and bridges. Lectric also equips the bike with hydraulic disc brakes and front and rear lights. The XP Lite2 is also great for RVers and campgrounds, since it’s lightweight (about 48 pounds) and folds down to 36x16x27-inch dimensions.

Sources indicate that many “step-through” e-bikes don’t actually have a low step design. This makes it challenging for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, by REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. The CTY is a great choice for older riders, those with reduced mobility, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

It has been revealed that REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor that provides smooth pedal-assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem for a comfortable riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for better stopping. For less than the cost of some e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI warranty and service.

The Current ADV is the priciest bike in this story, but for a good reason. Some electric bikes look a lot like mountain bikes, but that doesn’t mean they are built for real off-road use. Aventon’s new Current is the brand’s first full suspension E-MTB, and it is trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, stated, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers.”.

The Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor with 750 peak Watts and 110 Nm of torque. (It also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and 120 Nm of torque.) Rounding out the ADV are high-end components like a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

It has been revealed that in his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab particularly likes the Current’s easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data as well as the ability to tune the motor settings. If you don’t need rear suspension, check out Aventon’s updated Ramblas ADV hardtail E-MTB.

READ AVENTON CURRENT REVIEWMORE GREAT E-MTBs.

Recent findings suggest that getting into E-MTB trail riding on a budget is tough. Low-priced electric mountain bikes often aren’t built strong enough for off-road riding (or weigh half a rider’s weight), and trail-capable models typically cost more than $4,000. That’s what makes the TrailRush a standout bike—for less than $2,000, you get a trail-ready hardtail you can take on singletrack and have some fun.

In a recent development, ride1Up equips the 29-inch-wheeled TrailRush with a Brose mid-drive motor. With 90 Nm of torque, it isn’t as powerful as many new, higher-priced E-MTB motors, but it gets the job done. The TrailRush also comes stock with a dropper seatpost, four-piston disc brakes, and tubeless-compatible rims with Maxxis Minion tires.

In a recent development, of course, to hit this great price, Ride1Up made some equipment sacrifices. The 504Wh battery isn’t as large as some peers (like the Aventon Ramblas), so you get less ride time between charges. Additionally, the 11-36T cassette and 38T chainring limit your ability to climb steep hills.

Compared to earlier iterations of the Aventure, the third-generation model has a smoother ride and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s upcoming torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found earlier models had too much torque, but this Aventure remedied that fault. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

It has been revealed that the Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-roading, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths, but with this burly bike’s weight and components, it has limited functionality on singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers the Aventure M, a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price. Those refinements cost about $1,000 more than the Aventure 3.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have limited mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike technology, but it lets you get out and enjoy some rides without breaking the bank.

It has been revealed that I combed through dozens of Amazon listings comparing low-priced electric bikes, and this Heybike stood out for its combination of price and features. Then, I saw someone on the local bike path with one and asked them about the bike. The rider liked it and said it has been trouble-free (they noted a local bike shop assembled it for them). Heybike’s U.S. support line is available for warranty service or product questions.

In a recent development, don’t want to purchase from Amazon? Use this exclusive Bicycling discount link for $100 (applied at checkout) off the Cityscape 2.0, plus free shipping.

Tern’s cargo bikes are the gold standard for practical features, durability, and ride quality. This reputation makes the brand’s GSD (longtail) and HSD (short-tail) cargo models top picks for bike commuters, families, and riders looking to cut their dependence on automobiles.

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example of this is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

Recent findings suggest that many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. At the moment priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it boasts an impressive 60-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. (The dual-battery model for $1,799 doubles the range to 120 miles.) This makes the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around and a good option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

In a recent development, “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, remarked Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

However, to reach a price like this, concessions have to be made somewhere. This results in a somewhat cheap feeling to the bike. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but at times, it feels erratic. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend buying.

Sources indicate that plenty of commuter e-bikes cost far less than Specialized’s Turbo Vado SL 2, and they can probably do most of these things. So why spend twice as much as many popular options? I dive into the details in my story, “Stop Wasting Money on Cheap E-Bikes. Here’s Why Spending More Pays Off for Commuters.”.

In a recent development, the TL;DR: The Turbo Vado SL 2’s excellent ride geometry, silky-smooth motor, low weight, and premium components make riding fun. Together, these features make you want to ride the Vado every day and use it for more than simply getting to work. And thanks to Specialized’s extensive dealer network, you have somewhere to turn when it needs service.

Sources indicate that “Lightweight e-bike” might sound like an oxymoron to some, but a sub-40-pound weight is impressive when many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds. And often, e-bikes this light are pricey. Yet, the Velotric Tempo is only $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight.

Velotric achieves this weight reduction by ditching the bulky suspension fork (suspension forks on lower-priced bikes often don’t work all that well, to be frank), swapping heavy tires for 700x42c gravel tires, and using a smaller battery. Riders who need to carry the bike up any stairs or load it onto a bike rack will appreciate the reduced weight. However, heavier riders may want to test ride the Tempo before purchase, as lower-powered motors can bog down and reduce battery range for bigger-bodied people.

Sources indicate that bicycles are my life, and I’m a dedicated e-bike user and enthusiast. I’ve also worked in cycling for over 25 years. For almost six years, I’ve ridden and tested electric bikes as Bicycling’s Deputy Editor—and I use e-bikes for my daily commute. Before joining the staff, I led product development for top bicycle brands.

Our editors test dozens of electric bikes across every cycling category, and we continually receive latest models to evaluate. Our riding involves much more than taking bikes on short spins; we use electric bikes in our daily lives. Commuting, school drop-offs, grocery runs, and daily transportation are only a few of the things we regularly do with e-bikes. We also hit the trails on E-MTB models to test their performance in real-world mountain biking conditions, not simply riding them around town.

In addition to ride-testing, our editors regularly talk to cyclists of all ages and abilities about their riding needs. This helps us craft our list of Best Electric Bikes: e-bikes that will meet your needs on the street, trails, and around the neighborhood. Two of the e-bikes in this story even made the final cut for our 2026 Bike Awards.

It has been revealed that electric bike prices range from entry-level models for less than $500 to premium machines costing almost as much as a good used car. However, our years of testing have proven that many of the best and most practical models live squarely in the middle.

We find that many standout e-bikes are priced between $1,500 and $3,000. These models strike a good balance between reliability and practicality, without requiring you to overspend on features or technology you don’t need. Electric bikes costing less than $1,000 often take shortcuts to achieve this, either by using lower-quality parts or offering limited service after the bike is purchased.

According to recent reports, of course, you can also spend much more on electric bikes. Premium e-bikes typically offer improved motor performance, higher-quality components, lower weight, or more tech features. However, for most general riding purposes, these bikes are overkill—but they‘re certainly fun!

→ Consider how much cargo you’ll need to carry if your riding involves commuting or running errands. Look for a bike with appropriate racks, mount points, and other accessories.

→ For singletrack and trail riding, look for mountain bikes with knobby tires, adjustable suspension, high-quality frames, and low weight.

Recent findings suggest that → Pay attention to weight. While fat tire e-bikes and cargo bikes offer versatility, many weigh over 90 pounds. If you’ll need to carry your bike up any stairs or lift it onto a bike rack, a lighter option will be a better fit.

→ Bike storage is another consideration. While most e-bikes don’t require excessive space compared to their non-pedal-assisted counterparts, ensure you have access to a power outlet where you plan to store it for easy charging.

It has been revealed that several e-bike brands, Aventon, Ride1Up, and Lectric, performed well in our ride testing and evaluations. These bikes might require some minor assembly at home, such as installing pedals, a seat, and tightening handlebars. We considered how easy bikes were to assemble in our recommendations. Many bike shops will not assemble or otherwise work on e-bikes they do not sell due to liability issues. The direct-to-consumer brands we recommend have dealers nationwide ready to support you.

Industry observers note that established bike companies, such as Specialized and Trek, manufacture e-bikes and have hundreds of dealers across North America. Additionally, REI sells its house-brand Co-op electric bikes (and models from Cannondale and Tern) in its stores.

According to recent reports, there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding your bike.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

What this means: Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows people to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Other countries classify electric bikes differently, and many do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Electric bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. Mid-drive e-bikes tend to be more expensive, but are typically more reliable and higher performance. Because the extra weight on a mid-drive motor is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors.

According to recent reports, measured in Newton meters (or Nm), torque is a rotational measurement of force—and the number to pay attention to when you want an idea of an e-bike motor’s output. More torque means more power off the line and more boost to your pedaling.

Industry observers note that the heavier the bike, the more torque it needs. Lighter road bikes typically have 30 to 40 Nm of torque, and trail and cargo models (generally) have at least 80 Nm. Most commuter bikes fall somewhere in between.

In a recent development, the size of an e-bike’s battery is measured in watt-hours (or Wh). This measurement represents the energy stored in the battery and how many watts it can deliver each hour. The higher the number, the longer the range, but the faster you go, the faster you drain the battery.

So, if a 504Wh battery paired with a 500W motor gives you one hour of ride time at the highest assist, riding at about half that power will double your range.

Many e-bike brands seamlessly integrate batteries to make the bike look sleeker (and more like a traditional non-assist bike). Most batteries lock to the bike and come with a key that lets you unlock and remove it, which serves multiple purposes: You can remove the battery and charge it off the bike, plus a locked battery deters (and hopefully prevents) a thief from stealing it. An e-bike with the battery removed is safer for hauling on a bike rack and lighter for carrying up steps.

Since e-bikes can maintain higher speeds for longer than standard bikes, you want extra control when riding. Wider tires provide better traction and the freedom to leave the pavement with little penalty, and a suspension fork will help tame some of the rougher roads you might explore. Good disc brakes are a must, too, for slowing a heavy bike at high speed. This is not a place to skimp.

Industry observers note that some e-bikes have an integrated lighting system that turns on when you power up the bike. While this is a great feature, it’s not a deal-breaker if your bike doesn’t come equipped this way. It’s just as easy to attach your own since so many great bike lights are available.

E-bikes need regular maintenance and repair to stay in good working condition. Because they’re heavier and go faster than non-assist bicycles, e-bikes often require more regular service on parts like brakes, tires, and drivetrain components. We recommend having a good relationship with a local bike shop experienced in e-bike repair to keep your equipment running smoothly.

E-bikes use electronics for their motors, batteries, and displays. These parts are often proprietary to bike brands or even specific e-bike models, making replacement more difficult than parts on non-electric bicycles. Make sure to use the correct electronic replacement parts to avoid damaging your e-bike (or it catching fire).

In a recent development, established brands usually (but not always) have a good supply of these parts for replacement, even for years after a bike goes out of production. Bosch and Shimano are two e-bike motor manufacturers with some of the most compatibility between bikes and stock parts for previous generations of systems.

It has been revealed that look for e-bikes from brands that offer at least a one-year warranty on electronic components (many brands’ warranties are longer) and make items like replacement batteries for your bike. These parts are usually not cheap (sometimes up to half the cost of a newly introduced bike), but it’s the difference between having an e-bike that can be repaired or becomes a bicycle-shaped paperweight if something goes wrong.

Following a dramatic increase in fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes, there is a push from local officials, regulatory agencies, and advocacy groups across the U.S. for improved safety certification of e-bikes, batteries, and motor units. In September 2023, a Newly introduced York City law took effect requiring that any e-bike sold in the city “has been certified by an accredited testing laboratory for compliance with Underwriters Laboratories (UL) standard 2849”.

According to recent reports, however, just because something is marketed as UL 2849 compliant, tested to UL 2849, or even “certified to UL 2849” does not mean it is UL Safety Certified. Ibrahim Jilani, UL’s Global Director of Consumer Technology, notes: “Certification is always earned by a manufacturer and not a given when they undergo a product submittal. The UL Mark, or any authorized certification mark, can only be issued upon successful demonstration of meeting the requirements of the safety standard.” You can find UL’s updated list of products certified to UL 2849 here. You can cross-reference OSHA’s Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories for a deep dive into the topic.

According to recent reports, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Newly introduced England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success.
  • Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World.
  • Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success. Go out too hard and you may struggle to hold on. Run too conservatively and you might miss your goal finish.

Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World. One workout he recommends for building this skill is a fartlek he learned from fellow run coach Brad Hudson, his coauthor on the book, Run Faster from the 5K to the Marathon: How to Be Your Own Best Coach.

Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them. The goal? Building both aerobic fitness and a greater sense of pace control.

This workout helps improve your ability to settle into the right effort earlier, as well as enhance your capacity to hold those paces for longer—a perfect session for both optimizing your weekly speed run and helping you run your fastest race.

After an easy running warmup, you’ll run five faster segments, separated by an easy jog of the same duration.

The base workout uses three target paces: 5K pace for the one-minute segments, 10K pace for the two-minute segments, and half-marathon pace for the three-minute segment. If you don’t know your race paces, you can also go off of rate of perceived exertion (RPE), with 10 equaling all-out effort. You should still be able to have a conversation around 4 RPE.

Fitzgerald says the workout should feel “fun hard,” meaning the faster running should feel challenging, but you shouldn’t finish the workout feeling like you just went all out in a race. Each surge is relatively short, so focus on hitting your intended effort rather than pushing as hard as you can.

More experienced, higher-volume runners can extend the pyramid to 1-2-3-2-1-2-3-2-1, again jogging for the same duration after each faster segment. This version includes 17 minutes of faster running and 17 minutes of recovery jogging, compared to just nine minutes of each in the original version.

In Fitzgerald’s experience, many runners tend to think of their effort in two broad categories: slow and fast, but this workout challenges that by demanding more care in differentiating between faster paces.

The one-minute 5K pace efforts should be faster than the two-minute 10K pace efforts, which should be faster than the three-minute half-marathon effort, explains Fitzgerald. The differences between these three paces are small—often just a few seconds per mile—so learning to recognize what each one feels like can help you become a more efficient and more confident runner.

It has been revealed that before each segment, think about the effort you’re trying to find. For the first one-minute interval, Fitzgerald suggests literally imagining that you’re starting a 5K race. You wouldn’t want to sprint the opening minute of that race and flame out, so resist that urge here, too.

Try to settle into the right pace by feel, then use your watch to check and adjust. Over time, you’ll grow more attuned to the connection between how you feel and how fast you’re moving. “Your watch can’t [run the workout] for you,” Fitzgerald claims. “It can tell you how fast you’re going. It can’t tell you how fast you should go.”.

Sources indicate that learning to run by feel translates to race day, when you want to hit your goal pace. Your body’s response to the conditions and the effort helps you decide how to proceed through each mile, slowing down or speeding up.

This workout doesn’t ask you to spend a long time at any single pace. Instead, it gives you short exposures to several intensities within one session.

Hudson, who’s coached multiple Olympians and world-class athletes, tells Runner’s World that moving through a range of paces during a single workout helps with not only pace control, but also running economy or the energy required to run at a given speed.

Additionally, Hudson explains the continuous nature of the fartlek session gives it an aerobic emphasis because you never actually stop running throughout the entirety of the workout. “The faster portions [of the workout] increase oxygen demand, but as you go longer in a workout, the more it becomes aerobic, no matter what,” he indicates. “If you’re keeping the running continuous, the aerobic energy systems just keep going up and up and up.”.

According to recent reports, fitzgerald agrees, although he also notes athletes get some anaerobic stress during the shorter, faster efforts. Think of it as a way to work on several aspects of your fitness at once, rather than a session designed to train just one. Plus, switching between paces can make the workout more mentally engaging than returning to the same effort over and over again.

The first time you try the workout, you might overshoot a target pace or find it difficult to feel the difference between efforts. That’s okay. Fitzgerald indicates trial and error is an important part of developing the skill.

In a recent development, when you repeat the session, look for signs that your pacing is becoming more controlled: You start each segment closer to your intended effort, settle into a steadier rhythm, and maintain a clear difference between your 5K, 10K, and half marathon paces. You may also find it easier to keep your recovery jogs consistent.

The point is, you don’t need to nail every second of this workout. Learn from your mistakes, adjust when necessary, and remember Fitzgerald’s advice: “Progress over perfection.”.

Industry observers note that it may be tempting to think of the easy jogs simply as passing time between hard segments. But both coaches emphasize the value of continuous running and implore runners not to lose focus during the recovery intervals.

Industry observers note that fitzgerald says teaching your body to recover from a faster effort while still moving presents a unique challenge. Your muscles must learn how to continue producing the energy needed to keep you running efficiently while your body works to recover from the harder interval at the same time. This adaptation translates directly to race day when you have to settle back into race pace after surging to pass another runner or gliding a little too fast down a hill.

It has been revealed that the key is paying attention to how your recovery intervals feel. If you have to slow them down more and more to prepare for the next segment, Fitzgerald says that may be a sign you’re pushing the faster portions too hard.

The beauty of this workout is if you realize you’ve gone out too rapidly, you can easily adjust so you can still complete the workout. If you overcooked one of your speedier segments, Fitzgerald suggests tacking on another minute or so to the easy jog until you breathe easier and lower your heart rate—then adjust your effort level on the next interval.

Because the workout touches several intensity levels, Fitzgerald recommends it during base training or in the off-season. It can help runners maintain well-rounded fitness before they begin building toward a more specific goal.

It has been revealed that it can also work as the de facto speed workout during a lighter training week or serve as a secondary quality workout during half-marathon or marathon training. In this case, the session offers a chance to maintain some faster running while the biggest emphasis remains on your long runs and race-specific efforts.

Hudson uses the workout as a key tool in returning to training post-marathon. After a week off, he generally has his athletes begin with easy running. Then, he adds this workout as a way to reintroduce different intensity levels and prepare his athletes for more demanding work ahead.

Whenever you use it, keep its purpose in mind: It’s designed to help you practice changing gears and build general fitness, and using it to support key workouts specifically tailored to your next race makes it even more effective.

When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

Breaking: Frugal Man Buys $52,000 Car – Why??
